title: What it Means Being On-Call? - Google SRE
content:
| Topic | Extracted information | |---|---| | Operational runbook / SOP structure | - At the start of each shift, the on-call engineer reads the handoff from the previous shift.
- The on-call engineer minimizes user impact first, then makes sure the issues are fully addressed.
- At the end of the shift, the on-call engineer sends a handoff email to the next engineer on-call.
- The guidelines also specified when to escalate to others, and how to write postmortems for large incidents.
- The team read and updated on-call playbooks. | | Recurring security / compliance task execution | - Not explicitly stated as security/compliance tasks.
- Daily on-call handoffs were read.
- Weekly production meetings were attended.
- Monthly service review meeting was implemented.
- Morning review of incidents at a daily stand-up.
- Regular production meetings were run with the team and developer teams supported.
- Regular destructive testing or fuzzing was recommended.
- Regular load testing was recommended in addition to integration and unit testing.
- Run staging in a production-like environment.
- Perform canarying in a production environment.
- Run “Wheel of Misfortune” exercises.
- Hold regular meetings between the SRE team and developer team to discuss current production state and outstanding production bugs. | | Audit evidence / artifacts | - Daily on-call handoffs.
- Postmortems.
- On-call playbooks.
- Monitoring consoles.
- Dashboards.
- Service documentation.
- Disaster scenarios used during Google’s disaster recovery training week.
- Recordings of “Wheel of Misfortune” sessions for future reference.
- Incident ticket attached to any P1 or P2 event.
- Ticket used for event triage, tracking remediation actions, SLO impact, number of occurrences, and postmortem doc links, where applicable.
- Placeholder bug for each paging alert in the bug tracking system (e.g., Jira, IssueTracker).
- Link between paging alerts and the relevant bug in the bug tracking system.
- Searchable timeline of change information.
- Reports produced from structured data about causes of pages. | | POA&M / remediation records | - Incident ticket attached to any P1 or P2 event used for tracking remediation actions.
- Postmortem doc links, where applicable, included on incident ticket.
- Placeholder bug filed for each paging alert in bug tracking system.
- File a project bug in your team’s production component to surface engineering work that improves the system and obviates an entire class of possible future bugs.
- The team discussed remediation actions when pager budget was exceeded.
- Follow-up action items should be cataloged and tracked after serious paging events warranting postmortems.
- The Connection team adopted a strict policy requiring every outage to have a tracking bug.
- The technical program manager examined the root cause of new bugs in aggregate using that tracking bug data. | | RACI / role responsibilities | - SREs diagnose, mitigate, fix, or escalate incidents as needed.
- SRE teams mitigate incidents, repair production problems, and automate operational tasks.
- On-call engineers are human points of contact for escalations.
- On-call responder assesses impact to users when an event pages (P1).
- For Sev 1 incidents, the incident manager is paged, a scribe and communications lead is elected, and communication channels open.
- For Sev 2 or Sev 3, the on-call responder handles the incident lifecycle, including an abbreviated postmortem for incident review.
- SREs own the site operation.
- SREs define a shared roadmap for reliability, drive the full resolution of issues, and maintain monitoring rules.
- Feature developers are necessary collaborators but do not own these endeavors.
- Action items are assigned only to the five DevOps engineers—who are now SREs.
- SREs work with subject experts, many of them feature developers, to accomplish tasks.
- SREs send code reviews to the subject experts.
- The technical program manager and the people manager of the team approached senior management with a project proposal.
- SRE managers and tech leads should make sure that production bugs are promptly dealt with, and escalate to the developer team decision makers when necessary.
- When introducing a new paging alert, anyone on the team can write a new alert, but the whole team reviews proposed alert additions and can suggest alternatives.
- On-call engineers should update the playbook with fresh information when the corresponding page fires.
- Team members should follow up with each other when handoffs don’t adhere to expectations. | | Task / ticket / playbook templates | - On-call playbooks contain high-level instructions on how to respond to automated alerts.
- Playbooks explain the severity and impact of the alert.
- Playbooks include debugging suggestions and possible actions to take to mitigate impact and fully resolve the alert.
- Whenever an alert is created, a corresponding playbook entry is usually created.
- Each alert should have a corresponding playbook entry.
- Any P1 or P2 event has an incident ticket attached to it.
- The ticket is used for event triage and tracking remediation actions, as well as for SLO impact, number of occurrences, and postmortem doc links, where applicable.
- File a placeholder bug for each paging alert in the bug tracking system.
- Create a link between the paging alerts from the monitoring system and the relevant bug in the bug tracking system.
- The event triage/remediation/postmortem workflow references incident tickets. | | Escalation / exception handling | - The guidelines specified when to escalate to others.
- At three months, the Mountain View team became the primary on-call, with the Kirkland SREs as backup.
- The team could easily escalate to the Kirkland SREs if needed.
- The on-call engineer is never alone; ask a colleague to review findings.
- For Sev 1 incidents, the incident manager is paged, a scribe and communications lead is elected, and communication channels open.
- For events rating Sev 2 or Sev 3, the on-call responder handles the incident lifecycle, including an abbreviated postmortem.
- If a page is serious enough to warrant a postmortem, follow the methodology to catalog and track follow-up action items.
- If the problem cannot be identified, add monitoring and/or logging to help find the root cause the next time it occurs.
- If at all possible, avoid changes that can’t be rolled back, such as API-incompatible changes and lockstep releases.
- Use feature isolation to disable feature X without affecting feature Y.
- Drain requests away from elements of the system exhibiting the bug.
- Relaxing alert thresholds is rarely an appropriate response to being paged when fully subscribing to SLO-based and symptom-based alerting.
- New paging alerts should be explicitly approved or disallowed as a team.
- If introducing a new paging alert causes the service to exceed its paging budget, the stability of the system needs additional attention.
- Nonurgent swaps are typically best-effort.
- Teams with a strict pager response SLO need commute coverage.
- The policy for swaps should be documented.
- Peer review of schedule changes provides a good tradeoff between safety and flexibility.
- A team member can temporarily leave the rotation for long-term breaks.
- Teams should allow on-callers to temporarily leave the rotation because of changes in personal circumstances or burnout. | | Cadence / frequency | - Set period of being on-call.
- Typical shift length examples: per day or per week.
- One shift is 12 hours.
- Google’s maximum of two distinct incidents per 12-hour shift.
- We target a maximum of two incidents per on-call shift.
- The Mountain View team reviewed a checklist during onboarding before going on-call.
- After two months, Sara, Mike, and the SRE transfer shadowed the on-call shifts of the outgoing Kirkland SRE team.
- At three months, they became the primary on-call.
- Weekly production meetings.
- Daily on-call handoffs.
- Daily stand-up with morning incident review.
- Monthly service review meeting.
- A week of testing is probably about right for new alerts, depending on the alert and the system.
- A 21-day trailing average was found to be useful for pager load trends.
- Google has hundreds of on-call rotations across services of all sizes.
- The team in overload had regularly been receiving five paging incidents per shift for the past year.
- Fully one-third of shifts were exceeding their pager budget.
- The new SRE team’s monitoring improvements targeted 99.98% availability, or roughly 26 minutes of downtime per quarter.
- For 99.99% availability, approximately 15 minutes of error budget per quarter.
- For 99.999% availability, error budget of 80 seconds per quarter.
- New SRE hires were not expected to be ready for on-call before three to nine months.
- The team held lab sessions and “deep dives” during ramp-up.
- The team still held “Wheel of Misfortune” sessions after ramp-up, rotating through each team member as the session leader. | | Fields captured | - Incident ticket fields/uses: event triage, tracking remediation actions, SLO impact, number of occurrences, postmortem doc links, where applicable.
- Severity values: Sev 1, Sev 2, Sev 3.
- P1, P2, P3 classifications.
- Response time examples in Table 8-1: 5 minutes, 30 minutes, Ticket (response during work hours).
- SLO / SLA values and related numbers: 99.98% availability, 26 minutes of downtime per quarter, 99.99% availability, 15 minutes of error budget per quarter, 99.999% availability, 80 seconds per quarter, maximum two incidents per shift, one shift is 12 hours, 3 working weeks or 120 working hours, page costs on average 4 working hours.
- Pager budget and pager budget exceedance.
- Trigger rate during the testing period for new alerts.
- Alert severity and impact in playbooks.
- Data collection expectations for pages.
- Links between paging alerts and bugs.
- Searchable timeline of change information.
- Structured data about causes of pages.
- 21-day trailing average for pager load trends.
- Warning threshold for pager load.
- Personal preferences and historical on-call load per engineer in scheduling automation.
- Schedules must never change once generated. | | Tables | **Table 8-1. Examples of realistic response times**
|Incident description|Response time|SRE impact|
|--|--|--|
|Revenue-impacting network outage|5 minutes|SRE needs to be within arm's reach of a charged and authenticated laptop with network access at all times; cannot travel; must heavily coordinate with secondary at all times|
|Customer order batch processing system stuck|30 minutes|SRE can leave their home for a quick errand or short commute; secondary does not need to provide coverage during this time|
|Backups of a database for a pre-launch service are failing|Ticket (response during work hours)|None| | | Absence notes | - No explicit POA&M template heading was present.
- No explicit RACI matrix table was present.
- No explicit security or compliance task list was present.
- No explicit exception record form or escalation ticket template was present.
description: How Google Site Reliability Engineering teams structure on-call rotations, site operations, structure approaches to handle incidents and production issues.
author: Ollie Cook; Sara Smollett; Andrea Spadaccini; Cara Donnelly; Jian Ma; Garrett Plasky; Stephen Thorne; Jessie Yang

title: Google SRE - IT Service Management: Automate Operations
content:
| Topic | Extracted information | |---|---| | Operational runbook / SOP structure | - Google SRE relies on on-call playbooks.
- Thinking through and recording the best practices ahead of time in a “playbook” produces roughly a 3x improvement in MTTR as compared to the strategy of “winging it.”
- Clear and thorough troubleshooting steps and tips are valuable when responding to a high-stakes or time-sensitive page.
- Google SRE also uses exercises such as the “Wheel of Misfortune” to prepare engineers to react to on-call events. | | Recurring security/compliance task execution | - No explicit security or compliance task execution details are stated. | | Audit evidence / artifacts | - Postmortems should be written for all significant incidents, regardless of whether or not they paged.
- Postmortems that did not trigger a page are even more valuable, as they likely point to clear monitoring gaps.
- The investigation should establish what happened in detail, find all root causes of the event, and assign actions to correct the problem or improve how it is addressed next time.
- Logs are recorded for diagnostic or forensic purposes.
- No one needs to look at logs unless something else prompts them to do so. | | POA&M / remediation records | - Postmortems should assign actions to correct the problem or improve how it is addressed next time.
- No explicit POA&M record template or named remediation register is stated. | | RACI / role responsibilities | - SRE teams are responsible for the availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response, and capacity planning of their services.
- SRE teams interact with the production environment, product development teams, testing teams, users, and so on.
- Google places a 50% cap on the aggregate “ops” work for all SREs: tickets, on-call, manual tasks, etc.
- SREs spend the remaining 50% of time on development work.
- Operational work can be redirected to product development teams by reassigning bugs and tickets to development managers, [re]integrating developers into on-call pager rotations, and so on.
- The SRE team must be in charge of capacity planning, which means they also must be in charge of provisioning.
- SREs and product developers monitor and modify a service to improve performance, adding capacity and improving efficiency. | | Task / ticket / playbook templates | - Playbook (no explicit template headings stated).
- Postmortem (no explicit template headings stated).
- Monitoring output categories: Alerts, Tickets, Logging. | | Escalation / exception handling | - Alerts signify that a human needs to take action immediately in response to something that is either happening or about to happen, in order to improve the situation.
- Tickets signify that a human needs to take action, but not immediately; if a human takes action in a few days, no damage will result.
- SREs may redirect excess operational work to the product development teams.
- Reassigning bugs and tickets to development managers, [re]integrating developers into on-call pager rotations, and so on.
- If more than two events occur regularly per on-call shift, problems can’t be investigated thoroughly and engineers are sufficiently overwhelmed to prevent them from learning from these events.
- If on-call SREs consistently receive fewer than one event per shift, keeping them on point is a waste of their time.
- Once an error budget is depleted, one example response is to stop releases for the remainder of the quarter; this might not be embraced by a product development team unless mandated by management. | | Cadence / frequencies / thresholds | - Google caps operational work for SREs at 50% of their time.
- Google’s rule of thumb is that an SRE team must spend the remaining 50% of its time actually doing development.
- On average, SREs focused on operations work should receive a maximum of two events per 8–12-hour on-call shift.
- Postmortems should be written for all significant incidents.
- Roughly 70% of outages are due to changes in a live system.
- Capacity planning should include regular load testing of the system.
- Load shifting is often done multiple times per hour.
- 50–60% of SREs are Google Software Engineers.
- 40–50% of SREs are candidates very close to Google Software Engineering qualifications, with 85–99% of the skill set required, plus rare technical skills useful to SRE. | | Fields captured / named values | - Availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response, capacity planning.
- Root causes of the event.
- Actions to correct the problem or improve how it is addressed next time.
- Alert / Ticket / Logging.
- Mean time to failure (MTTF).
- Mean time to repair (MTTR).
- Error budget = one minus the availability target.
- A service that’s 99.99% available is 0.01% unavailable.
- Capacity planning inputs: organic growth and inorganic growth.
- Mandatory capacity planning steps: accurate organic demand forecast extending beyond lead time required for acquiring capacity; accurate incorporation of inorganic demand sources into the demand forecast; regular load testing to correlate raw capacity (servers, disks, and so on) to service capacity. | | Tables / phase structure | - No explicit operational phase table is stated.
- The page uses section headings: Introduction; The Sysadmin Approach to Service Management; Google’s Approach to Service Management: Site Reliability Engineering; Tenets of SRE; Ensuring a Durable Focus on Engineering; Pursuing Maximum Change Velocity Without Violating a Service’s SLO; Monitoring; Emergency Response; Change Management; Demand Forecasting and Capacity Planning; Provisioning; Efficiency and Performance; The End of the Beginning. | | Severity / SLA / availability values | - 100% is not the right reliability target for basically everything, with pacemakers and anti-lock brakes being notable exceptions.
- 99.999% availability is contrasted with 100% availability; the marginal difference is described as not benefiting the user in most cases.
- A service that’s 99.99% available is 0.01% unavailable.
- Error budget is one minus the availability target.
- The decision to stop releases for the remainder of the quarter once an error budget is depleted is mentioned as an example. | - No explicit named security/compliance audit schedule, exception approval workflow, RACI matrix, ticket template headings, or POA&M form fields are stated on the page.
description: SRE's approach to IT Service Management, Use software engineers to design scalable and reliable systems. Innovation and improve product development.
author: Benjamin Treynor Sloss

title: OPS07-BP03 Use runbooks to perform procedures - Operational Excellence Pillar
content:
- **Runbook definition and purpose**
  - A runbook is a documented process to achieve a specific outcome.
  - Runbooks consist of a series of steps that someone follows to get something done.
  - In cloud operations, runbooks are used to reduce risk and achieve desired outcomes.
  - At its simplest, a runbook is a checklist to complete a task.
  - Runbooks are an essential part of operating a workload.
  - Runbooks provide consistent outcomes no matter who uses them.
  - Runbooks should be published in a central location.
  - Runbooks should be updated as the process evolves.
  - Updating runbooks is a key component of a change management process.
  - Runbooks should include guidance on error handling, tools, permissions, exceptions, and escalations in case a problem occurs.

- **Desired outcome**
  - Your team has a collection of step-by-step guides for performing workload tasks.
  - The runbooks contain the desired outcome.
  - The runbooks contain necessary tools and permissions.
  - The runbooks contain instructions for error handling.
  - The runbooks are stored in a central location (version control system).
  - The runbooks are updated frequently.
  - Example capability: runbooks provide capabilities for teams to monitor, communicate, and respond to AWS Health events for critical accounts during application alarms, operational issues, and planned lifecycle events.

- **Common anti-patterns**
  - Relying on memory to complete each step of a process.
  - Manually deploying changes without a checklist.
  - Different team members performing the same process but with different steps or outcomes.
  - Letting runbooks drift out of sync with system changes and automation.

- **Benefits**
  - Reducing error rates for manual tasks.
  - Operations are performed in a consistent manner.
  - New team members can start performing tasks sooner.
  - Runbooks can be automated to reduce toil.

- **Level of risk exposed if this best practice is not established**
  - Medium

- **Implementation guidance**
  - At a minimum, runbooks should consist of a step-by-step text document.
  - The desired outcome should be clearly indicated.
  - Clearly document necessary special permissions or tools.
  - Provide detailed guidance on error handling and escalations in case something goes wrong.
  - List the runbook owner.
  - Publish the runbook in a central location.
  - Validate the runbook by having someone else on your team run it.
  - As procedures evolve, update runbooks in accordance with your change management process.
  - As the organization matures, text runbooks should be automated.
  - AWS Systems Manager automations can transform flat text into automations that can be run against your workload.
  - Automations can be run in response to events, reducing the operational burden to maintain your workload.
  - AWS Systems Manager Automation provides a low-code visual design experience to create automation runbooks more easily.

- **Customer example**
  - AnyCompany Retail must perform database schema updates during software deployments.
  - The Cloud Operations Team worked with the Database Administration Team to build a runbook for manually deploying these changes.
  - The runbook listed each step in the process in checklist form.
  - It included a section on error handling in case something went wrong.
  - They published the runbook on their internal wiki along with their other runbooks.
  - The Cloud Operations Team plans to automate the runbook in a future sprint.

- **Implementation steps**
  1. If you don't have an existing documentation repository or wiki, create a new version control repository in your version control system.
  2. Identify a process that does not have a runbook.
  3. An ideal process is one that is conducted semiregularly, short in number of steps, and has low impact failures.
  4. In your document repository, create a new draft Markdown document using the template.
  5. Fill in Runbook Title and the required fields under Runbook Info.
  6. Starting with the first step, fill in the Steps portion of the runbook.
  7. Give the runbook to a team member.
  8. Have them use the runbook to validate the steps.
  9. If something is missing or needs clarity, update the runbook.
  10. Publish the runbook to your internal documentation store.
  11. Once published, tell your team and other stakeholders.
  12. Over time, build a library of runbooks.
  13. As the library grows, start working to automate runbooks.

- **Level of effort for the implementation plan**
  - Low
  - The minimum standard for a runbook is a step-by-step text guide.
  - Automating runbooks can increase the implementation effort.

- **Runbook template**
  - **Template heading:** `# Runbook Title`
  - **Template heading:** `## Runbook Info`

| Runbook ID | Description | Tools Used | Special Permissions | Runbook Author | Last Updated | Escalation POC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RUN001 | What is this runbook for? What is the desired outcome? | Tools | Permissions | Your Name | 2022-09-21 | Escalation Name |

  - **Template heading:** `## Steps`
  - `1. Step one`
  - `2. Step two`

- **Runbook Info fields captured**
  - Runbook ID
  - Description
  - Tools Used
  - Special Permissions
  - Runbook Author
  - Last Updated
  - Escalation POC

- **Resources**
  - Related best practices:
    - OPS02-BP02 Processes and procedures have identified owners
    - OPS07-BP04 Use playbooks to investigate issues
    - OPS10-BP01 Use a process for event, incident, and problem management
    - OPS10-BP02 Have a process per alert
    - OPS11-BP04 Perform knowledge management
  - Related documents:
    - Achieving Operational Excellence using automated playbook and runbook
    - AWS Systems Manager: Working with runbooks
    - Migration playbook for AWS large migrations - Task 4: Improving your migration runbooks
    - Use AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks to resolve operational tasks
  - Related videos:
    - AWS re:Invent 2019: DIY guide to runbooks, incident reports, and incident response
    - How to automate IT Operations on AWS | Amazon Web Services
    - Integrate Scripts into AWS Systems Manager
  - Related examples:
    - Well-Architected Labs: Automating operations with Playbooks and Runbooks
    - AWS Blog Post: Build a Cloud Automation Practice for Operational Excellence: Best Practices from AWS Managed Services
    - AWS Systems Manager: Automation walkthroughs
    - AWS Systems Manager: Restore a root volume from the latest snapshot runbook
    - Building an AWS incident response runbook using Jupyter notebooks and CloudTrail Lake
    - Gitlab - Runbooks
    - Rubix - A Python library for building runbooks in Jupyter Notebooks
    - Using Document Builder to create a custom runbook
  - Related services:
    - AWS Systems Manager Automation

- **Explicit absences**
  - No POA&M records are provided.
  - No remediation records are provided.
  - No RACI table is provided.
  - No ticket template is provided.
  - No playbook template is provided.
  - No recurring security/compliance task cadence is provided beyond “frequently,” “semiregularly,” and “as procedures evolve.”
  - No severity or SLA values are provided.
description: A runbook is a documented process to achieve a specific outcome. Runbooks consist of a series of steps that someone follows to get something done. Runbooks have been used in operations going back to the early days of aviation. In cloud operations, we use runbooks to reduce risk and achieve desired outcomes. At their simplest, a runbook is a checklist to complete a task.

title: PagerDuty Incident Response Documentation
content:
## Operational runbook / SOP structure
| Section | Listed pages / topics | Descriptions explicitly stated |
|---|---|---|
| Home | PagerDuty Incident Response Documentation | “This documentation covers parts of the PagerDuty Incident Response process.” “It is a cut-down version of our internal documentation used at PagerDuty for any major incidents and to prepare new employees for on-call responsibilities.” “It provides information not only on preparing for an incident, but also what to do during and after the incident.” “It is intended to be used by on-call practitioners and those involved in an operational incident response process (or those wishing to enact a formal incident response process).” |
| Being On-Call | Being On-Call; Alerting Principles | “A guide to being on-call, both what your responsibilities are, and what they are not.” “The principles we use to determine what things page an engineer, and what time of day they page.” |
| Before an Incident | What is an Incident?; Severity Levels; Different Roles for Incidents; Incident Call Etiquette; Complex Incidents | “Before we can talk about incident response, we need to define what an incident actually is.” “Information on our severity level classification. What constitutes a SEV-3 vs SEV-1? What response do they get?” “Information on the roles during an incident(i.e. Incident Commander (IC), Scribe, etc.)” “Our etiquette guidelines for incident calls (before you find yourself in one).” “Our guide for handling larger, more complex incidents.” |
| During an Incident | During an Incident; Security Incident Response | “Information and processes during a major incident.” “Security incidents are handled differently than normal operational incidents.” |
| After an Incident | After an Incident; Postmortem Process; Postmortem Template; Effective Postmortems | “Our followup-processes, how we make sure we don't repeat mistakes, and are always improving.” “Information on what to do after an incident is resolved.” “Information on our postmortem process, what's involved, and how to write or run a postmortem.” “The template we use for writing our postmortems for major incidents.” “A guide for writing effective postmortems.” |
| Crisis Response | Introduction; Terminology; Crisis Leadership; Crisis Response Operations; Pre-crisis Phase; PagerDuty for CRMOps | “Incident response is about more than dealing with technical incidents.” “A crisis can happen at any time.” “How you handle your worst day will leave lasting impressions about your brand and its perceived value in the eyes of your current and potential customers.” “An introduction to crisis response and who this document is intended for.” “A list of key terms and concepts used in this guide.” “Incorporating basic principles and your values in your response.” “Activating your crisis response plans.” “Capitalizing on preparedness activities to keep your teams ready and engaged.” “How PagerDuty leverages PagerDuty for crisis response management operations.” |
| Training | Training Overview; Glossary of Incident Response Terms | “An overview of our training guides and additional training material from third parties.” “A collection of terms that you may hear being used along with their definitions.” |
| Training Guides | Incident Commander Training; Deputy Training; Scribe Training; Subject Matter Expert Training; Customer Liaison Training; Internal Liaison Training | “A guide to becoming an Incident Commander.” “How to be a Deputy and back up the Incident Commander.” “A guide to Scribing.” “A guide on responsibilities and behavior for all participants in a major incident.” “A guide on how to act as our public representative during an incident.” “A guide on how to liaise with internal teams during an incident.” |
| Training Courses | Incident Response Training Course | “An introductory course on incident response and the role of the Incident Commander (IC).” |
| Additional Resources | Reading; ChatOps; Anti-Patterns | “Recommended reading material relevant to incident response.” “Description of the chat bot commands we've referenced in this documentation.” “List of things we've tried and then rejected - learn from our mistakes.” |

## Recurring security / compliance task execution

- Crisis Response Operations: “Activating your crisis response plans.”
- Pre-crisis Phase: “Capitalizing on preparedness activities to keep your teams ready and engaged.”
- After an Incident: “Our followup-processes, how we make sure we don't repeat mistakes, and are always improving.”

- No POA&M, remediation record, or equivalent record format is explicitly stated on this page.
- After an Incident: “how we make sure we don't repeat mistakes, and are always improving.”

## RACI / role responsibilities

| Incident Commander (IC) | Mentioned in “Different Roles for Incidents” as one of the roles during an incident. Mentioned in “Incident Response Training Course” as “the role of the Incident Commander (IC).” |
| Scribe | Mentioned in “Different Roles for Incidents” as one of the roles during an incident. Mentioned in “Scribe Training” as “A guide to Scribing.” |

title: incident-response-docs/docs/during/security_incident_response.md at master · PagerDuty/incident-response-docs
content:
- **Document**
  - `security_incident_response.md`
  - Cover description: `Checklist of actions for responding to a security incident at PagerDuty.`
  - **Last Reviewed:** `YYYY-MM-DD`
  - **Last Tested:** `YYYY-MM-DD`

- **Operational structure / escalation**
  - **Incident Commander Required**
    - Security incidents involve an **Incident Commander** who will delegate tasks to relevant responders.
    - Tasks may be performed in parallel as assigned by the IC.
    - Page one at the earliest possible opportunity: `!ic page`
  - **Not Sure it's a Security Incident?**
    - Trigger the process anyway.
    - The Incident Commander will make a determination on if response is needed.

- **Checklist**
  1. Stop the attack in progress.
  2. Cut off the attack vector.
  3. Assemble the response team.
  4. Isolate affected instances.
  5. Identify timeline of attack.
  6. Identify compromised data.
  7. Assess risk to other systems.
  8. Assess risk of re-attack.
  9. Apply additional mitigations, additions to monitoring, etc.
  10. Forensic analysis of compromised systems.
  11. Internal communication.
  12. Involve law enforcement.
  13. Reach out to external parties that may have been used as vector for attack.
  14. External communication.

- **Attack Mitigation**
  - Stop the attack as quickly as you can, via any means necessary.
  - Shut down servers, network isolate them, turn off a data center if you have to.
  - Common actions:
    - Shutdown the instance from the provider console.
    - Do not delete or terminate if you can help it, as forensic analysis will be needed.
    - If logged into the box:
      - Reinstate default iptables rules to restrict traffic.
      - `kill -9` any active session you think is an attacker.
      - Change root password and update `/etc/shadow` to lock out all other users.
      - `sudo shutdown now`

- **Cut Off Attack Vector**
  - Identify the likely attack vectors and path/fix them so they cannot be re-exploited immediately after stopping the attack.
  - If a third-party provider is suspected compromised:
    - Delete all accounts except your own and those of others who are physically present.
    - Immediately rotate your password and MFA tokens.
  - If a service application was an attack vector:
    - Disable any relevant code paths.
    - Or shut down the service entirely.

- **Assemble Response Team**
  - Identify the key responders for the security incident and keep them all in the loop.
  - Set up a secure method of communicating all information associated with the incident.
  - Details on the incident, or even the fact that an incident has occurred, should be kept private to responders until confident the attack is not being triggered internally.
  - **Actions**
    - Page an Incident Commander if not already done so.
    - They will appoint the usual incident command roles.
    - The incident command team will be responsible for keeping documentation of actions taken.
    - The incident command team will be responsible for notifying internal stakeholders as appropriate.
    - Give the project an innocuous codename for chats/documents.
      - Example: `sapphire-unicorn`
    - Start the voice call if not already in progress.
    - Setup chat room using the codename of the incident.
    - Invite all responders to the voice call and chat room.
      - The security team should always be included.
      - A representative for any affected services should be included.
      - Executive stakeholders and legal counsel should be invited at earliest possible opportunity, but prioritize operational responders first.
    - Do not communicate with anyone not on the response team about the incident until forensics have been performed.
    - Prefix all emails and chat topics with `Attorney Work Project`.

- **Isolate Affected Instances**
  - Any instances affected by the attack should be immediately isolated from any other instances.
  - As soon as possible, an image of the system should be taken and put into a read-only cold storage for later forensic analysis.
  - **Actions**
    - Blacklist the IP addresses for any affected instances from all other hosts.
    - Turn off and shutdown the instances immediately if not already done to stop the attack.
    - Take a disk image for any disks attached to the instances.
    - Ship the disk images to an off-site cold storage location.
    - Make sure these images are read-only and cannot be tampered with.

- **Identify Timeline of Attack**
  - Work with all tools at your disposal to identify the timeline of the attack and exactly what the attacker did.
  - **Capture**
    - Any reconnaissance the attacker performed on the system before the attack started.
    - When the attacker gained access to the system.
    - What actions the attacker performed on the system, and when.
    - How long the attacker had access to the system before they were detected.
    - How long the attacker had access to the system before they were kicked out.
    - Any queries the attacker ran on databases.
    - Whether the attacker still has access to the system via another back door.
    - Monitor logs for unusual activity.

- **Compromised Data**
  - Using forensic analysis of log files, time-series graphs, and any other information/tools at your disposal, attempt to identify what information was compromised, if any.
  - **Capture**
    - Any data that was compromised during the attack.
      - Was any data exfiltrated from a database?
      - What keys were on the system that are now considered compromised?
      - Was the attacker able to identify other components of the system (map out the network, etc)?
    - Find exactly what customer data has been compromised, if any.

- **Assess Risk**
  - Based on the data that was compromised, assess the risk to other systems.
  - **Capture**
    - Does the attacker have enough information to find another way in?
    - Were any passwords or keys stored on the host?
      - If so, they should be considered compromised regardless of how they were stored.
    - Any user accounts that were used in the initial attack should rotate all of their keys and passwords on every other system they have an account.

- **Apply Additional Mitigations**
  - Start applying mitigations to other parts of your system.
  - **Actions**
    - Rotate any compromised data.
    - Identify any new alerting which is needed to notify of a similar breach.
    - Block any IP addresses associated with the attack.
    - Identify any keys/credentials that are compromised and revoke their access immediately.

- **Forensic Analysis**
  - Once confident the systems are secured and enough monitoring is in place to detect another attack, move onto the forensic analysis stage.
  - **Actions**
    - Take any read-only images created and any access logs available, and comb through them for more information about the attack.
    - Identify exactly what happened, how it happened, and how to prevent it in future.
    - Keep track of all IP addresses involved in the attack.
    - Monitor logs for any attempt to regain access to the system by the attacker.

- **Internal Communication**
  - **Delegate to:** `VP or Director of Engineering`
  - Communicate internally only once confident, via forensic analysis, that the attack was not sourced internally.
  - **Actions**
    - Don't go into too much detail.
    - Overview the timeline.
    - Discuss mitigation steps taken.
    - Follow up with more information once it is known.

- **Liaise With Law Enforcement / External Actors**
  - **Delegate to:** `VP or Director of Engineering`
  - Work with law enforcement to identify the source of the attack.
  - Let any system owners know that systems under their control may be compromised.
  - **Actions**
    - Contact local law enforcement.
    - Contact the FBI.
    - Contact operators for any systems used in the attack; their systems may also have been compromised.
    - Contact security companies to help in assessing risk and any PR next steps.
    - Contact your cyber insurance provider.

- **External Communication**
  - **Delegate to:** `Marketing Team`
  - Once all information is validated as accurate, timeline of events is known, exactly what information was compromised and how it was compromised is known, and it is certain it won't happen again, prepare and release a public statement to customers.
  - The public statement should inform customers of the compromised information and any steps they need to take.
  - **Actions / fields**
    - Include the date in the title of any announcement so that it is never confused for a potential new breach.
    - Don't say `"We take security very seriously."`
    - Be honest, accept responsibility, and present the facts, along with exactly how the company plans to prevent such things in future.
    - Be as detailed as possible with the timeline.
    - Be as detailed as possible in what information was compromised and how it affects customers.
    - If storing something that should not have been stored, be honest about it.
    - Don't name and shame any external parties that might have caused the compromise.
    - If they have already publicly disclosed, link to their disclosure.
    - Release the external communication as soon as possible, preferably within a few days of the compromise.
    - If possible, get in touch with customers' internal security teams before the general public notice is sent.

- **Communicating During an Incident**
  - Prefer voice call and Slack over any other methods.
  - Avoid email.
    - If email is absolutely needed:
      - Subject of emails should be `Attorney Work Project` and nothing else.
      - If the email chain has **ANY** contacts not with the `@pagerduty.com` domain, make sure emails are encrypted.
  - Do not use SMS to communicate about the incident.
    - Only exception: to tell someone to move to a more secure channel, e.g. `Please join Slack ASAP.`
  - Do not disseminate anything about the incident to those outside the response team until approval to do so.

- **Additional Reading**
  - `Computer Security Incident Handling Guide` (NIST)
  - `Incident Handler's Handbook` (SANS)
  - `Responding to IT Security Incidents` (Microsoft)
  - `Defining Incident Management Processes for CSIRTs: A Work in Progress` (CMU)
  - `Creating and Managing Computer Security Incident Handling Teams (CSIRTS)` (CERT)

title: How to create an incident response playbook
content:
## Incident response playbook structure and SOP content

### Purpose and uses
- Incident response playbooks are described as:
  - Standard procedures and steps for responding and resolving incidents in real time.
  - Including peacetime training and exercises to prepare the team for the next incident.
- Playbooks are a key component of DevOps and IT Ops incident management, as well as cybersecurity.
- Playbooks set the organization’s policies and practices for responding to unplanned outages.
- Playbooks help teams bring order to chaos and make sure everyone responds to incidents and security threats consistently.
- An incident management handbook gives the team a set of processes for responding to, resolving, and learning from every incident, whether it is a security issue or another emerging vulnerability.
- Content can include:
  - runbooks
  - checklists
  - templates
  - training exercises
  - security attack scenarios
  - simulation drills

### The article’s 5 incident response playbook steps
1. Define incidents for your organization
2. Establish predesignated roles
3. Enforce a consistent process
4. Enable rapid response
5. Facilitate comprehensive postmortems

## Definitions and incident scope

### “What is an Incident?”
- An incident is defined as:
  - an event that causes disruption to or a reduction in the quality of a service which requires an emergency response
- Teams who follow ITIL or ITSM practices may use the term:
  - “major incident”

### Resolution and postmortem boundary
- An incident is resolved when the affected service resumes functioning in its usual way.
- This includes only tasks required to restore full functionality.
- This excludes follow-on tasks such as:
  - root cause identification
  - mitigation
- Those excluded tasks are part of the postmortem.
- The incident postmortem is done after the incident to:
  - determine the root cause
  - assign actions to ensure it is addressed before it can cause a repeat incident

## Roles and responsibilities

### Roles used at Atlassian
| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Incident Manager | Has overall responsibility and authority for the incident. Empowered to take any action necessary to resolve the incident, which includes paging additional responders in the organization and keeping those involved in an incident focused on restoring service as quickly as possible. |
| Tech Lead | A senior technical responder. Responsible for developing theories about what is broken and why, deciding on changes, and running the technical team. Works closely with the incident manager. |
| Communications Manager | A person familiar with public communications, possibly from the customer support team or public relations. Responsible for writing and sending internal and external communications. |

### Role design intent
- Roles and responsibilities are designated to ensure:
  - all necessary steps are covered
  - no duplicate work occurs
  - communication runs smoothly and effectively
- Individuals on the incident response team are familiar with each role and know what they are responsible for during an incident.

## Process structure, phases, and flow

### Consistent process guidance
- Outline key steps and phases.
- Make sure team members are clear on:
  - what is expected during each phase
  - what comes next
- Atlassian outlines the incident response flow over:
  - seven steps
  - three phases
- The flow is intended to drive the incident from:
  - detection
  - to resolution

### Process description
- As a new incident is detected:
  - the incident manager begins initiating internal communication
  - the incident manager begins response organization
- Then the team works on:
  - fixing the cause of the incident
  - reaching a resolution
- Strong organization in this stage facilitates action, which is powered by frequent communication.
- Adhering to a consistent process leads to:
  - faster resolution
  - a postmortem exercise

## Templates, checklists, and rapid-response aids

### Rapid response guidance
- Incident playbooks need to be simple enough for teams to follow in times of stress.
- Atlassian’s process includes a major incident manager “cheat sheet.”
- The cheat sheet outlines key steps like:
  - assessment
  - escalation
  - delegation
- The cheat sheet is in a one-page format.

### Play / training reference
- Try running an Incident Response Values play.
- Purpose:
  - improve team cohesiveness
  - work out potential misunderstandings prior to an incident
- Use the Atlassian Team Playbook to better understand the team’s process in order to build a dynamic playbook.

## Postmortem and remediation records

### Postmortem purpose
- A postmortem seeks to maximize the value of an incident by:
  - understanding all contributing causes
  - documenting the incident for future reference and pattern discovery
  - enacting effective preventative actions to reduce the likelihood or impact of recurrence

### Postmortem methods used at Atlassian
- Face-to-face meetings
  - help drive appropriate analysis
  - align the team on what needs fixing
- Postmortem approvals
  - by delivery and operations team managers
  - incentivize teams to do them thoroughly
- Designate priority actions
  - with assigned Service Level Objectives (SLO)
  - with reminders and reports to ensure they are completed

### Postmortem reference
- A step-by-step outline of the Atlassian incident response postmortem can be found on:
  - page 46 of the Incident Management Handbook

## Audit evidence / artifacts explicitly mentioned
- Incident Management Handbook
- major incident manager “cheat sheet”
- Incident Response Values play
- Atlassian Team Playbook
- postmortem documentation
- reminders and reports for assigned priority actions with SLO
- page 46 of the Incident Management Handbook for the postmortem outline

## Cadence, frequency, and timing
- Peacetime training and exercises are included in playbooks.
- Incident teams are constantly:
  - training
  - refining
  - testing
  - improving
- Frequent communication is emphasized during incident response.
- “No one has time to debate best practices” when an incident occurs.
- There are no explicit recurring frequencies, schedules, or SLA values stated beyond:
  - assigned Service Level Objectives (SLO)
  - reminders and reports to ensure completion

## POA&M / remediation tracking
- The page does not explicitly use the terms POA&M, remediation record, or ticketing system.
- What is available:
  - postmortem assigns actions
  - priority actions are designated
  - actions are assigned Service Level Objectives (SLO)
  - reminders and reports ensure completion

## Fields captured / issue fields
- The page states that the postmortem includes:
  - outline of the postmortem process
  - issue fields
- No specific issue field names are listed in the page.

## Escalation and exception handling
- The major incident manager cheat sheet outlines:
  - assessment
  - escalation
  - delegation
- Incident Manager may page additional responders in the organization.
- The playbook should be flexible and adapt to changing situations.
- Incidents are scenarios where things do not go according to plan.

## Directly stated numbered/structured content

### Atlassian’s 5 best practices for managing an incident
1. Define incidents for your organization
2. Establish predesignated roles
3. Enforce a consistent process
4. Enable rapid response
5. Facilitate comprehensive postmortems

- Seven steps
- Three phases
- Drives the incident from detection to resolution

title: Playbook templates for Jira Service Management
content:
- **Page title:** Playbook templates for Jira Service Management
- **Availability / plans:**
  - Playbook templates are available on **Jira Service Management Premium** and **Enterprise** plans.
- **Purpose / structure:**
  - Playbook templates help standardize common ITSM, IT Operations, and HR service workflows without building playbooks from scratch.
  - Each template provides a ready-made structure that combines guided steps and automation to help agents resolve work items consistently and efficiently.
  - Designed for Jira Service Management admins who want to standardize operational processes and reduce errors in complex workflows.
  - Each template includes:
    - a predefined set of steps (instructional and/or automation rule steps)
    - automation steps mapped to reusable automation rule templates where applicable
  - You can start from a template and customize it to match your team’s tools, policies, and workflows.
- **Access / navigation:**
  - Go to **Space settings > Playbooks > Templates**.
  - You can preview templates and start creating a playbook with prefilled fields.

## IT Operations playbook templates

| Template name | Use when | Typical steps include |
|---|---|---|
| High CPU on Amazon RDS | An Amazon RDS database instance shows sustained or unexpected CPU spikes affecting performance. | check RDS CPU metrics; retrieve instance details; analyze slow queries; scale or reboot the DB instance; validate CPU reduction; document findings |
| Jenkins deployment failure | A Jenkins deployment fails and requires immediate investigation and containment. | fetch the latest Jenkins build status; review deployment logs; validate Jenkins system health |
| Major incident response plan (planned) | An incident has high business impact and requires cross-team coordination. | identify service owners; gather response resources; communicate with leadership; manage Statuspage updates; initiate post-incident review |
| Manage change rollback | A deployment or change needs to be reverted to restore service. | prepare rollback and notify stakeholders; execute rollback; verify rollback success; communicate results |
| Manage stakeholder communications | An incident requires timely, consistent external communication. | confirm affected services; create incident on Statuspage; post status updates; close the incident |
| Restart service with Azure runbook | A service restart is required to mitigate an incident. | check logs and health metrics; notify stakeholders; start Azure runbook; verify service health; communicate outcome |

## ITSM playbook templates

| Template name | Use when | Typical steps include |
|---|---|---|
| Provision software license | A user requests access to licensed software or a specific role. | check user roles and entitlements; check existing access; request manager approval (optional); provision access; notify the requester |

## HR Service Management (HRSM) templates

| Template name | Use when | Typical steps include |

| IT setup for new employee | A new employee joins and needs IT access and setup. | create employee account; provide group and tool access; create onboarding tasks; complete onboarding |

title: Resolve security threats with the playbook - ServiceNow
content:
- **Resolve security threats with the playbook**
  - **Release version:** Australia
  - **Updated:** March 12, 2026
  - **Read time:** 8 minutes
  - **Purpose:** Use the Playbook to resolve certain types of security threats in a step-by-step manner.
  - **Examples of threats:** phishing attacks; threats caused by malicious code activity.
  - **Role required:** `sn_si.admin` or `admin`

- **Playbook structure / phases / task flow**
  - Each group of tasks:
    - Analysis
    - Contain
    - and so forth
  - Task groups guide the user through questions and activities for resolving the threat.
  - As tasks are completed, subsequent tasks are presented based on choices made.
  - Grayed out groups may be activated by choices made.
  - Example groups and purposes:
    - **Analysis**: determine the validity and scope of the threat.
    - **Contain**: isolate the threat to a specific user or asset.
    - **Eradicate**: remove malware or reimage the host.
    - **Recover**: mentioned as a possible grayed out group.
    - **Review**: mentioned as a possible grayed out group.
  - The playbook guides the user to the next state when all tasks for a state are completed.
  - Continue working on each task until all tasks are completed to resolve the threat and close the security incident.

- **Task execution details**
  - Enter **work notes** as each task is worked through to help analyze similar attacks in the future.
  - After a threat is identified, the playbook can be used to:
    - quarantine the threat
    - isolate similarly affected assets
    - remove malware
  - Knowledge articles:
    - included in each task
    - provide tips and other information to help perform needed steps
    - base system includes knowledge articles for each playbook task
    - custom knowledge articles can be written and associated with playbook tasks
  - Some tasks ask a question, such as:
    - `"Is Email Part of Campaign?"`
    - Perform necessary analysis and select **Yes** or **No**.
  - Some tasks are transitional and instruct the user to perform an action, such as:
    - adding observables to a security incident
    - after completing the action, click **Mark as Completed**
  - Knowledge articles appear when work on a task starts, if associated.

- **Security incident selection / filtering**
  - Security Incidents screen shows security incidents assigned to the user.
  - Filter options:
    - **Assigned to me**
    - all open incidents
    - all unassigned incidents
  - Quick Filters can be used to view incidents of a particular type, such as:
    - only Critical incidents
  - Consider prioritizing security incidents with **high risk scores**.
  - If the playbook pane on the right-hand edge is closed, click the playbook icon to open it.
  - If no playbook is assigned:
    - select a playbook from the **Selected Playbook** choice list
    - assign a different playbook to the security incident
  - Phishing category security incident:
    - Phishing Playbook is automatically available
    - select the playbook icon to open the playbook

- **Phishing playbook**
  - Tasks help analyze, contain, and eradicate a phishing threat.
  - Tasks are organized into states:
    - Analysis
    - Contain
    - and so forth
  - When all tasks for a state are completed, the playbook guides the user to the next state.
  - **Recover task:** not used in the Phishing playbook.

- **How security incidents are created from user-reported phishing attacks**
  - During Security Incident Response setup, the system administrator creates a series of **email matching rules** that identify emails containing signs of phishing.
  - Employees receiving a suspicious email can send it as an **.EML attachment** to the phishing email address defined by the organization.
  - When received:
    - the .EML attachment is parsed
    - its information is compared to the email matching rules
    - if a match is found, a security incident is created
  - Security incident created contains:
    - **Short description** includes `User Reported Phishing`, followed by the actual subject from the originating email
    - the **.EML file** is attached
    - if the .EML contained observables, they are parsed, and enrichment and threat lookups are automatically performed

- **Analysis state**
  - Tasks performed:
    - determine the validity of the incident
    - study the impact of the potential threat
    - coordinate an effective response to the incident
  - As tasks are worked through:
    - familiarize yourself with the knowledge articles
    - open the email attachment and examine it for common phishing elements
    - review threat lookup results

- **Contain state**
  - Tasks review the details of the email.
  - To ensure threats cannot enter the organization, update network defenses in the form of:
    - Intrusion Defense System (IDS) signatures and rules
    - Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) signatures and rules
  - As tasks are worked through:
    - take actions to limit threat impacts, such as isolating the impacted devices
    - examine the observables attached to the email
    - determine whether any email contents are associated with a known threat, including:
      - URL
      - Email sender
      - Phishing URL
      - IP address of the sender's SMTP server

- **Eradicate state**
  - After updated signatures and rules are deployed to the antivirus solution, use tasks to determine if malware is present and handle it accordingly.
  - As tasks are worked through:
    - scan the endpoints of affected devices for the presence of malware
    - remove any malware found
    - as a last resort, wipe and reimage the host devices

- **Review state**
  - If a phishing attack is determined to be a false alarm during Analysis:
    - the security incident moves to the Review state
    - users need to be notified so they know it is safe to open the email attachment

- **Closed state**
  - When all tasks in the playbook have been completed:
    - the security incident is moved to the Closed state
    - **closing comments must be entered before the incident can be closed**

- **Cancelled state**
  - When a security incident is in the Review state and users have been successfully informed that the email is not a threat:
    - the Cancelled state becomes active
    - the security incident can be cancelled

- **Associate a knowledge article with a playbook task**
  - **Role required:** `sn_sir.knowledge_admin`, and either `sn_si.admin` or `admin`
  - Before beginning:
    - note the text associated with each task
    - example first task in the Phishing category: `Was Alert Employee-Submitted?`
    - this is the short description of the task
    - exact text is needed to associate a knowledge article
  - Procedure:
    1. Navigate to .
    2. Create and publish a knowledge article for a specific playbook task.
    3. Navigate to .
    4. Create a runbook, filling in the following information:
       | Field | Description |
       |---|---|
       | Knowledge article | Select the published knowledge article you want to associate with the playbook task. |
       | Table | Select Security Incident Response Task `[sn_si_task]`. |
       | Condition | Set the condition builder to: |
       | Condition - Option | Select Short description. |
       | Condition - Operator | Select is. |
       | Condition - Input value | Enter the short description for the task, exactly as it appears in the playbook. |
    5. Click Submit.
  - Result:
    - the next time you run the playbook and select this task, the associated knowledge article is displayed

- **Add a custom task to the playbook**
  - The Security Analyst Workspace base system includes a series of tasks for each threat category.
  - Custom tasks can be created to meet the unique needs of the system or customers.
  - **Role required:** `sn_si.basic` or `security_admin`
  - Procedure:
    1. With the playbook open, select **Add Task**.
    2. The **Add Custom Task** screen opens.
    3. Fill in the fields, as needed.

  - **Add Custom Task screen fields**
    | Field | Description |
    |---|---|
    | Number | [Read only] The automatically-generated security incident task number. |
    | Parent | The number of the related security incident. |
    | Configuration item | The configuration item affected by the security issue, if any. |
    | Affected user | The user affected by the security issue, if any. |
    | Priority | Select the priority used to determine when this task should be performed. |
    | Security Incident State | The current state of the security response task. You can select a future state, if needed. |
    | Outcome type | If you have the `sn_si.basic` role, select Yes/No as the outcome type. If you have the `security_admin` role, you can create a custom outcome type with multiple custom output values. For example, you can define a task with dependant values based on the threat category. |
    | Assignment group | The assignment group from which the assigned worker will be selected. |
    | Assigned to | The individual assigned to perform the task. |
    | Short description | A description of the Security Incident playbook task. |
    | Description | Enter a description for the selected task. |
  - After entries are completed, select **Add Task**.
  - The task is inserted in the playbook following the current task.

title: Incident response planning | Microsoft Learn
content:
## Operational runbook / SOP structure
- Use this table as a checklist to prepare your Security Operations Center (SOC) to respond to cybersecurity incidents.

| Done | Activity | Description | Benefit |
|--|--|--|--|
|  | Table top exercises | Conduct periodic table top exercises of foreseeable business-impacting cyber incidents that force your organization's management to contemplate difficult risk-based decisions. | Firmly establishes and illustrates cybersecurity as a business issue. Develops muscle memory and surfaces difficult decisions and decisions rights issues across the organization. |
|  | Determine pre-attack decisions and decision-makers | As a complement to table top exercises, determine risk-based decisions, criteria for making decisions, and who must make and execute those decisions. For example: Who/when/if to seek assistance from law enforcement? Who/when/if to enlist incident responders? Who/when/if to pay ransom? Who/when/if to notify external auditors? Who/when/if to notify privacy regulatory authorities? Who/when/if to notify securities regulators? Who/when/if to notify board of directors or audit committee? Who has authority to shut down mission-critical workloads? | Defines the initial response parameters and contacts to involve that streamline the response to an incident. |
|  | Maintaining privilege | Typically, advice can be privileged, but facts are discoverable. Train key incident leaders in communicating advice, facts and opinions under privilege so that privilege is preserved and risk is reduced. | Maintaining privilege can be a messy process when considering the multitude of communications channels, including e-mail, collaboration platforms, chats, documents, artifacts. For example, you can use Microsoft Teams Rooms. A consistent approach across incident personnel and supporting external organizations can help reduce any potential legal exposure. |
|  | Insider trading considerations | Contemplate notifications to management that should be taken to reduce securities violations risk. | Boards and external auditors tend to appreciate that you have mitigations that will reduce the risk of questionable securities trades during periods of turbulence. |
|  | Incident roles and responsibilities playbook | Establish basic roles and responsibilities that allow various processes to maintain focus and forward progress. When your response team is remote, it can require other considerations for time zones and proper handoff to investigators. You might have to communicate across other teams that might be involved, such as vendor teams. | **Technical Incident Leader** – Always in the incident, synthesizing inputs and findings and planning next actions. **Communications Liaison** – Removes the burden of communicating to management from the Technical Incident Leader so they can remain involved in the incident without loss of focus. This activity should include managing executive messaging and interactions with other third parties such as regulators. **Incident Recorder** – Removes the burden of recording findings, decisions, and actions from an incident responder and produces an accurate accounting of the incident from beginning to end. **Forward Planner** – Working with mission-critical business process owners, formulates business continuity activities and preparations that contemplate information system impairment that lasts for 24, 48, 72, 96 hours, or more. **Public Relations** – In the event of an incident that is likely to garner public attention, with Forward Planner, contemplates and drafts public communication approaches that address likely outcomes. |
|  | Privacy incident response playbook | To satisfy increasingly strict privacy regulations, develop a jointly owned playbook between SecOps and the privacy office. This playbook will allow rapid evaluation of potential privacy issues that might arising out of security incidents. | It's difficult to evaluate security incidents for their potential to impact privacy because most security incidents arise in a highly technical SOC. The incidents must quickly get surfaced to a privacy office (often with a 72-hour notification expectation) where regulatory risk is determined. |
|  | Penetration testing | Conduct point-in-time simulated attacks against business-critical systems, critical infrastructure, and backups to identify weaknesses in security posture. Typically, this activity is conducted by a team of external experts focused on bypassing preventative controls and surfacing key vulnerabilities. | In light of recent human-operated ransomware incidents, penetration testing should be conducted against an increased scope of infrastructure, particularly the ability to attack and control backups of mission-critical systems and data. |
|  | Red Team / Blue Team / Purple Team / Green Team | Conduct continuous or periodic simulated attacks against business-critical systems, critical infrastructure, backups to identify weaknesses in security posture. Typically, this activity is conducted by internal attack teams (Red teams) who are focused on testing the effectiveness of detective controls and teams (Blue teams). For example, you can use Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender XDR for Office 365 and Attack tutorials & simulations for Microsoft Defender XDR for Endpoint. | Red, Blue, and Purple team attack simulations, when done well, serve a multitude of purposes: - Allows engineers from across the IT organization to simulate attacks on their own infrastructure disciplines. - Surfaces gaps in visibility and detection. - Raises the security engineering skills across the board. - Serves as a more continuous and expansive process. The Green Team implements changes in IT or security configuration. |
|  | Business continuity planning | For mission-critical business processes, design and test continuity processes that allow the minimum viable business to function during times of information systems impairment. For example, use an Azure backup and restore plan to protect your critical business systems during an attack to ensure a rapid recovery of your business operations. | - Highlights the fact that there's no continuity workaround for the impairment or absence of IT systems. - Can emphasize the need and funding for sophisticated digital resilience over simpler backup and recovery. |
|  | Disaster recovery | For information systems that support mission-critical business processes, you should design and test hot/cold and hot/warm backup and recovery scenarios, including staging times. | Organizations that conduct bare metal builds often find activities that are impossible to replicate or don't fit into the service level objectives. Mission-critical systems running on unsupported hardware many times can't be restored to modern hardware. Restore of backups is often not tested and experiences issues. Backups may be further offline such that staging times haven't been factored into recovery objectives. |
|  | Out-of-band communications | Prepare for how you would communicate in the the following scenarios: - Email and collaboration service impairment - Ransom of documentation repositories - Unavailability of personnel phone numbers. | Although it's a difficult exercise, determine how to store important information immutably in off-line devices and locations for distribution at scale. For example: - Phone numbers - Topologies - Build documents - IT restoration procedures |
|  | Hardening, hygiene, and lifecycle management | In line with Center for Internet Security (CIS) Top 20 security controls, harden your infrastructure and perform thorough hygiene activities. | In response to recent human-operated ransomware incidents, Microsoft has issued specific guidance for protecting every stage of the cyberattack kill chain. This guidance applies to Microsoft capabilities or the capabilities of other providers. Of particular note are: - The creation and maintenance of immutable backup copies in the event of ransomed systems. You might also consider how to keep immutable log files that complicate the attacker's ability to cover their tracks. - Risks related to unsupported hardware for disaster recovery. |
|  | Incident response planning | At the outset of the incident, decide on: - Important organizational parameters. - Assignment of people to roles and responsibilities. - The sense-of-urgency (such as 24x7 and business hours). - Staff for sustainability for the duration. | There's a tendency to throw all available resources at an incident in the beginning, in the hope of a quick resolution. Once you recognize or anticipate that an incident will go for an extended period of time, take on a different posture that with your staff and suppliers that allows them to settle in for a longer haul. |
|  | Incident responders | Establish clear expectations with one another. A popular format of reporting ongoing activities includes: - What have we done (and what were the results)? - What are we doing (and what results will be produced and when)? - What do we plan to do next (and when is it realistic to expect results)? | Incident responders come with different techniques and approaches, including dead box analysis, big data analysis, and the ability to produce incremental results. Starting with clear expectations will facilitate clear communications. |

## RACI / role responsibilities
- **Technical Incident Leader** – Always in the incident, synthesizing inputs and findings and planning next actions.
- **Communications Liaison** – Removes the burden of communicating to management from the Technical Incident Leader so they can remain involved in the incident without loss of focus. This activity should include managing executive messaging and interactions with other third parties such as regulators.
- **Incident Recorder** – Removes the burden of recording findings, decisions, and actions from an incident responder and produces an accurate accounting of the incident from beginning to end.
- **Forward Planner** – Working with mission-critical business process owners, formulates business continuity activities and preparations that contemplate information system impairment that lasts for 24, 48, 72, 96 hours, or more.
- **Public Relations** – In the event of an incident that is likely to garner public attention, with Forward Planner, contemplates and drafts public communication approaches that address likely outcomes.

## Cadence / frequency
- **Periodic** table top exercises
- **Point-in-time** simulated attacks
- **Continuous or periodic** simulated attacks
- **72-hour notification expectation** for privacy office surface-up, as stated
- Incident response planning at the **outset of the incident**
- Forward Planner preparations for impairment lasting **24, 48, 72, 96 hours, or more**

## Audit evidence / artifacts
- Advice
- Facts
- Opinions under privilege
- E-mail
- Collaboration platforms
- Chats
- Documents
- Artifacts
- Executive messaging
- Interactions with other third parties such as regulators
- Findings
- Decisions
- Actions
- Accurate accounting of the incident from beginning to end
- Important information stored immutably in off-line devices and locations
- Phone numbers
- Topologies
- Build documents
- IT restoration procedures

## Escalation / exception handling
- Determine pre-attack decisions and decision-makers for:
  - seek assistance from law enforcement
  - enlist incident responders
  - pay ransom
  - notify external auditors
  - notify privacy regulatory authorities
  - notify securities regulators
  - notify board of directors or audit committee
  - authority to shut down mission-critical workloads
- Privacy incidents should quickly get surfaced to a privacy office; stated as often with a **72-hour notification expectation**
- Out-of-band communications scenarios:
  - Email and collaboration service impairment
  - Ransom of documentation repositories
  - Unavailability of personnel phone numbers

## Template headings / reporting structure
- A popular format of reporting ongoing activities includes:
  - What have we done (and what were the results)?
  - What are we doing (and what results will be produced and when)?
  - What do we plan to do next (and when is it realistic to expect results)?

## Fields captured
- Important organizational parameters
- Assignment of people to roles and responsibilities
- Sense-of-urgency (**24x7 and business hours**)
- Staff for sustainability for the duration
- Risk-based decisions
- Criteria for making decisions
- Who must make and execute those decisions
- Results
- When results will be produced
- When it is realistic to expect results

## Tables
### Key Microsoft security resources

| Resource | Description |
|--|--|
| 2021 Microsoft Digital Defense Report | A report that encompasses learnings from security experts, practitioners, and defenders at Microsoft to empower people everywhere to defend against cyberthreats. |
| Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures | A set of visual architecture diagrams that show Microsoft's cybersecurity capabilities and their integration with Microsoft cloud platforms such as Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Azure and third-party cloud platforms and apps. |
| Minutes matter infographic download | An overview of how Microsoft's SecOps team does incident response to mitigate ongoing attacks. |
| Azure Cloud Adoption Framework security operations | Strategic guidance for leaders establishing or modernizing a security operation function. |
| Microsoft security best practices for security operations | How to best use your SecOps center to move faster than the attackers targeting your organization. |
| Microsoft cloud security for IT architects model | Security across Microsoft cloud services and platforms for identity and device access, threat protection, and information protection. |
| Microsoft security documentation | Additional security guidance from Microsoft. |

## Explicit absence
- No POA&M or remediation records are provided.

description: This publication provides a methodology and set of procedures for conducting assessments of security and privacy controls employed within systems and organizations within an effective risk management framework. The assessment procedures, executed at various phases of the system development life cycle, are consistent with the security and privacy controls in NIST Special Publication 800-53, Revision 5. The procedures are customizable and can be easily tailored to provide organizations with the needed flexibility to conduct security and privacy control assessments that support organizational risk management processes and are aligned with the stated risk tolerance of the organization. Information on building effective security and privacy assessment plans is also provided with guidance on analyzing assessment results.
