title: Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information ...
content:
| Category | Extracted information |
|---|---|
| Publication | NIST Special Publication 800-53A Revision 5 |
| Title | Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations |
| Date | January 2022 |
| Scope | Methodology and set of procedures for conducting assessments of security and privacy controls employed within systems and organizations within an effective risk management framework |
| Key lifecycle phases explicitly referenced | initiation; development/acquisition; implementation; operations and maintenance; disposition (disposal) |
| Assessment lifecycle use | assessments are executed at various phases of the system development life cycle; routinely conducted during development/acquisition and implementation; conducted during operations and maintenance; conducted at end of life cycle for disposal |
| Related frameworks/publications | Risk Management Framework (RMF); [SP 800-37]; [SP 800-53]; [SP 800-53B]; [SP 800-39]; [SP 800-137]; [SP 800-47], Revision 1; [OMB A-130]; [FISMA]; [CNSSI 1253]; [FIPS 199]; [SP 800-60 Vol 1]; [SP 800-60 Vol 2]; [NARA CUI]; [FedRAMP]; [ISO 15408]; [FIPS 140-3] |
| Supplemental formats | assessment procedures in Chapter 4 are published in CSV, plain text, and OSCAL; available from publication details page and OSCAL Content Git Repository |

### Operational runbook / SOP structure and cadence

| Section / Step | Explicit content |
|---|---|
| Chapter Three process | prepare for security and privacy control assessments; develop security and privacy assessment plans; conduct security and privacy control assessments; analyze assessment report results; assess security and privacy capabilities |
| Table 1: Prepare step purpose | address a range of issues pertaining to the cost, schedule, scope, and performance of the control assessment |
| Table 1: Primary roles | Authorizing Official; Authorizing Official Designated Representative; system owner; common control provider; control assessors |
| Table 1: Supporting roles | System security officer; system privacy officer |
| Table 1: Outcomes | The objective, scope, and timeframe of control assessment determined; Key organizational stakeholders notified and necessary resources allocated; Assessors/assessment teams identified; Artifacts collected and provided to assessors/assessment teams; Mechanism to minimize ambiguities and misunderstandings about control implementation and identified control deficiencies or weaknesses established; Assessors/assessment teams understand the organization’s operations, structure, objective, scope, and timeframe of control assessment |
| Preparation activities by organization | ensuring appropriate policies covering security and privacy control assessments are in place and understood by all affected organizational elements; ensuring all steps in the RMF prior to the security or privacy control assessment step have been successfully completed and received appropriate management oversight; establishing objective and scope of assessments; ensuring common controls and common portion of hybrid controls assigned to appropriate organizational entities (common control providers) for development and implementation; notifying key organizational officials of impending assessments and allocating necessary resources; establishing appropriate communication channels among organizational officials with an interest in the assessments; establishing time frames for completing the assessments and key milestone decision points required by the organization; identifying and selecting appropriate assessors/assessment teams and considering issues of assessor independence; providing artifacts to assessors/assessment teams; establishing a mechanism between the organization and the assessors and/or assessment teams to minimize ambiguities or misunderstandings about implementation and related weaknesses or deficiencies |
| Preparation activities by assessors/assessment teams | obtaining a general understanding of the organization’s operations, including mission, functions, and business processes; obtaining an understanding of the structure of the system and the security and privacy controls being assessed; identifying the organizational entities responsible for development and implementation of the common controls or common portion of hybrid controls; meeting with appropriate organizational officials to ensure common understanding for assessment objectives and proposed rigor and scope; obtaining artifacts needed for the assessment; establishing appropriate organizational points of contact; obtaining previous assessment results that may be reused |
| Reuse / prior evidence | organizations are encouraged to take advantage of control assessment results and associated assessment documentation, artifacts, and evidence available for system components from previous assessments, including independent third-party testing, evaluation, and validation; previous assessment results may be appropriately reused for the current assessment; examples include Inspector General reports, audits, vulnerability scans, physical security inspections, developmental testing and evaluation, vendor flaw remediation activities, [ISO 15408] evaluations |
| Assessment plan inputs | information about controls to be assessed, including results from assessments of risk; platform-specific dependencies in hardware, software, or firmware; assessment procedures needed as a result of organization-specific controls not included in [SP 800-53] |
| Cadence / frequency | the frequency of assessments and monitoring is determined by the organization, system owner, and/or common control provider and is approved by the authorizing official; security and privacy controls are assessed on an ongoing basis in accordance with ISCM strategy and privacy continuous monitoring strategy |
| End-of-life / disposal | security and privacy assessments are conducted to ensure important organizational information, including personally identifiable information, are purged from the system prior to disposal and organizational retention schedules are adhered to |

### Roles / responsibilities / RACI-like content

| Role / party | Explicit responsibilities / notes |
|---|---|
| Authorizing Official | approves frequency of ongoing assessments and monitoring; makes risk-based decision on whether to place the system into operation or continue its operation |
| Authorizing Official Designated Representative | primary role in Prepare step |
| system owner | primary role in Prepare step; identifies and coordinates with other parties; may determine assessment frequency with common control provider; evaluates control assessment results; inheriting controls is not responsible for common control assessments |
| common control provider | primary role in Prepare step; responsible for common control assessments and assessments of the common part of hybrid controls |
| control assessors | primary role in Prepare step; conduct assessments and obtain evidence |
| system security officer | supporting role in Prepare step |
| system privacy officer | supporting role in Prepare step |
| system security and privacy officers | involved in assessments; listed among parties with oversight responsibilities |
| Inspectors General | individuals with information security and privacy assessment and monitoring responsibilities; may conduct assessments; use previous assessment results such as IG reports |
| auditors | individuals with assessment and monitoring responsibilities; listed among roles responsible for conducting control assessments |
| analysts | individuals with information security and privacy assessment and monitoring responsibilities |
| authorizing officials / chief information officers / senior information security officers / senior agency officials for privacy / chief privacy officers / system managers / information security and privacy managers | individuals with system, security, privacy, risk management, and oversight responsibilities |
| system owners / common control providers / information owners/stewards / mission and business owners / system administrators / system security officers / system privacy officers | individuals with information security and privacy implementation and operational responsibilities |
| mission and business owners | other interested parties in control assessments |
| information owners/stewards | other interested parties in control assessments when role is filled by someone other than the system owner |
| system developers | produce design/development artifacts and may participate in assessments/interviews |
| system integrators | listed among individuals with system development responsibilities |
| information security engineers / privacy engineers | listed among individuals with system development responsibilities |

### Evidence, artifacts, and audit/assessment outputs

| Artifact / evidence / record | Explicit use |
|---|---|
| policies | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects |
| procedures | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects |
| plans | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects; includes system security plans, privacy plans, configuration management plan |
| specifications | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects; includes system security and privacy requirements, functional specifications |
| designs | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects; includes architectural designs, system design documentation |
| records | provided to assessors/assessment teams; examined as assessment objects; includes administrator/operator manuals, system documentation, information exchange agreements, previous assessment results, legal requirements |
| administrator/operator manuals | provided to assessors/assessment teams |
| system documentation | provided to assessors/assessment teams |
| information exchange agreements | provided to assessors/assessment teams |
| previous assessment results | provided to assessors/assessment teams; reused for current assessment |
| legal requirements | provided to assessors/assessment teams |
| audit records | potential assessment objects for several controls |
| system monitoring records | potential assessment objects for AC-17(01) |
| system configuration settings and associated documentation | potential assessment objects for several controls |
| change control records | potential assessment objects for CM-04 and CM-02 |
| security impact analysis documentation | potential assessment object for CM-04 |
| privacy impact analysis documentation | potential assessment object for CM-04 |
| privacy impact assessment | potential assessment object for CM-04 |
| privacy risk assessment documentation | potential assessment object for CM-04 |
| system design documentation | potential assessment object for CM-04, CM-02, AC-17, AC-17(01), CA-03, MP-07 |

title: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring ...
content:
| Section | Extracted operational structure / recurring tasks / artifacts / roles / cadence / fields | |---|---| | Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) definition | - “maintaining ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities, and threats to support organizational risk management decisions” | | ISCM process steps | - Define an ISCM strategy
- Establish an ISCM program
- Implement an ISCM program
- Analyze data and Report findings
- Respond to findings
- Review and Update the ISCM strategy and program | | Chapter 3 process description | - Define an ISCM strategy based on risk tolerance that maintains clear visibility into assets, awareness of vulnerabilities, up-to-date threat information, and mission/business impacts
- Establish an ISCM program determining metrics, status monitoring frequencies, control assessment frequencies, and an ISCM technical architecture
- Implement an ISCM program and collect the security-related information required for metrics, assessments, and reporting; automate collection, analysis, and reporting where possible
- Analyze the data collected and Report findings, determining the appropriate response; additional information may be collected to clarify or supplement monitoring data
- Respond to findings with technical, management, and operational mitigating activities or acceptance, transference/sharing, or avoidance/rejection
- Review and Update the monitoring program, adjusting the ISCM strategy and maturing measurement capabilities to increase visibility into assets and awareness of vulnerabilities, further enable data-driven control of the security of an organization’s information infrastructure, and increase organizational resilience | | Tiers | - Tier 1 = organization
- Tier 2 = mission/business processes
- Tier 3 = information systems | | Tier 1 focus | - High-level information security governance policy as it relates to risk to the organization as a whole, its core missions, and its business functions
- Criteria for ISCM defined by the organization’s risk management strategy, including how the organization plans to assess, respond to, and monitor risk, and oversight required to ensure the strategy is effective | | Tier 2 focus | - Criteria for continuous monitoring defined by how core mission/business processes are prioritized with respect to the organization’s overall goals and objectives, the types of information needed to execute mission/business processes, and the organization-wide information security program strategy
- Controls in the Program Management (PM) family are an example of Tier 2 security controls | | Tier 3 focus | - Ensuring all system-level security controls (technical, operational, and management controls) are implemented correctly, operate as intended, produce the desired outcome, and continue to be effective over time
- Assessing and monitoring hybrid and common controls implemented at the system level
- Security status reporting may include security alerts, security incidents, and identified threat activities | | Primary ISCM governance roles | - Head of Agency
- Risk Executive (Function)
- Chief Information Officer (CIO)
- Senior Information Security Officer (SISO)
- Authorizing Official (AO)
- Information System Owner (ISO)/Information Owner/Steward
- Common Control Provider
- Information System Security Officer (ISSO)
- Security Control Assessor | | Head of Agency role | - Likely to participate in the organization’s ISCM program within the context of the risk executive (function) | | Risk Executive (Function) role | - Oversees the organization’s ISCM strategy and program
- Reviews status reports from the ISCM process as input to information security risk posture and risk tolerance decisions
- Provides input to mission/business process and information systems tier entities on ISCM strategy and requirements
- Promotes collaboration and cooperation among organizational entities
- Facilitates sharing of security-related information
- Provides an organization-wide forum to consider all sources of risk
- Ensures that risk information is considered for continuous monitoring decisions | | CIO role | - Leads the organization’s ISCM program
- Ensures that an effective ISCM program is established and implemented by establishing expectations and requirements
- Works closely with authorizing officials to provide funding, personnel, and other resources to support ISCM
- Maintains high-level communications and working group relationships among organizational entities | | SISO role | - Establishes, implements, and maintains the organization’s ISCM program
- Develops organizational program guidance (policies/procedures) for continuous monitoring of the security program and information systems
- Develops configuration management guidance for the organization
- Consolidates and analyzes POA&Ms to determine organizational security weaknesses and deficiencies
- Acquires or develops and maintains automated tools to support ISCM and ongoing authorizations
- Provides training on the organization’s ISCM program and process
- Provides support to information owners/information system owners and common control providers on how to implement ISCM for their information systems | | AO role | - Assumes responsibility for ensuring the organization’s ISCM program is applied with respect to a given information system
- Ensures the security posture of the information system is maintained
- Reviews security status reports and critical security documents
- Determines if the risk to the organization from operation of the information system remains acceptable
- Determines whether significant information system changes require reauthorization actions
- Reauthorizes the information system when required | | ISO / Information Owner / Steward role | - Establishes processes and procedures in support of system-level implementation of the organization’s ISCM program
- Develops and documents an ISCM strategy for the information system
- Participates in the organization’s configuration management process
- Establishes and maintains an inventory of components associated with the information system
- Conducts security impact analyses on changes to the information system
- Conducts, or ensures conduct of, assessment of security controls according to the ISCM strategy
- Prepares and submits security status reports in accordance with organizational policy and procedures
- Conducts remediation activities as necessary to maintain system authorization
- Revises the system-level security control monitoring process as required
- Reviews ISCM reports from common control providers to verify common controls continue to provide adequate protection
- Updates critical security documents based on ISCM results | | Common Control Provider role | - Establishes processes and procedures in support of ongoing monitoring of common controls
- Develops and documents an ISCM strategy for assigned common controls
- Participates in the organization’s configuration management process
- Establishes and maintains an inventory of components associated with the common controls
- Conducts security impact analyses on changes that affect the common controls
- Ensures security controls are assessed according to the ISCM strategy
- Prepares and submits security status reports in accordance with organizational policy/procedures
- Conducts remediation activities as necessary to maintain common control authorization
- Updates/revises the common security control monitoring process as required
- Updates critical security documents as changes occur
- Distributes critical security documents to individual information owners/information system owners, and other senior leaders in accordance with organizational policy/procedures | | ISSO role | - Supports the organization’s ISCM program by assisting the ISO in completing ISCM responsibilities
- Participates in the configuration management process | | Security Control Assessor role | - Provides input into the types of security-related information gathered as part of ISCM
- Assesses information system or program management security controls for the organization’s ISCM program
- Develops a security assessment plan for each security control
- Submits the security assessment plan for approval prior to conducting assessments
- Conducts assessments of security controls as defined in the security assessment plan
- Updates the security assessment report as changes occur during ISCM
- Updates/revises the security assessment plan as needed | | Other roles mentioned | - Information system administrator
- ISCM program manager | | Organization-wide ISCM strategy policies/procedures/templates | - Policy that defines key metrics
- Policy for modifications to and maintenance of the monitoring strategy
- Policy and procedures for the assessment of security control effectiveness (common, hybrid, and system-level controls)
- Policy and procedures for security status monitoring
- Policy and procedures for security status reporting (on control effectiveness and status monitoring)
- Policy and procedures for assessing risks and gaining threat information and insights
- Policy and procedures for configuration management and security impact analysis
- Policy and procedures for implementation and use of organization-wide tools
- Policy and procedures for establishment of monitoring frequencies
- Policy and procedures for determining sample sizes and populations and for managing object sampling
- Procedures for determining security metrics and data sources
- Templates for assessing risks
- Templates for security status reporting (on control effectiveness and status monitoring) | | Training requirements tied to ISCM roles | - Policies, procedures, and templates address manual and automated monitoring methodologies
- Organizations establish policy and procedures for training of personnel with ISCM roles
- Training may include management and use of automated tools, establishing baselines, tuning measurements, recognition of and appropriate response to triggers and alerts from metrics indicating risks beyond acceptable limits, and internal or external reporting requirements | | Expected inputs / outputs: Tier 1 & 2 strategy development | **Expected Input:** Organizational risk assessment and current risk tolerance; current threat information; organizational expectations and priorities; available tools from OMB lines of business and/or third-party vendors
**Expected Output:** Updated information on organizational risk tolerance; organization-wide ISCM strategy and associated policy, procedures, templates, tools | | Expected inputs / outputs: Tier 3 strategy development | **Expected Input:** Organizational risk tolerance information; organizational ISCM strategy, policy, procedures, templates; system-specific threat information; system information (e.g., System Security Plan, Security Assessment Report, Plan of Action and Milestones, Security Assessment Plan, System Risk Assessment, etc.)
**Expected Output:** System-level ISCM strategy that complements the Tier 1 and 2 strategies and the organizational security program and that provides security status information for all tiers and real-time updates for ongoing system authorization decisions as directed by the organizational ISCM strategy | | Required or cited artifacts / evidence | - System Security Plan
- Risk Assessment Report
- Security Assessment Report
- Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M)
- Hardware and software inventories
- Security Assessment Plan
- Security status reports
- Critical security documents
- Security-related information from assessments and monitoring
- Evidence needed for ongoing authorization decisions | | Ongoing authorization artifacts | - System Security Plan together with Risk Assessment Report, Security Assessment Report, and POA&M are kept up to date on an ongoing basis | | POA&M use | - POA&M resource and prioritization decisions
- Consolidated POA&M information used to determine common weaknesses/deficiencies among information systems
- Aggregate POA&M information used to allocate risk mitigation resources organization-wide and to make adjustments to the monitoring strategy
- Risk response implementation plans documented in the system’s POA&M
- Weaknesses found are evaluated and mitigation actions are conducted immediately or are added to the POA&M | | Analysis/reporting procedures | - Organizations develop procedures for analyzing and reporting assessment and monitoring results
- Procedures include specific staff/roles to receive ISCM reports, content and format of the reports, frequency of reports, and any tools to be used
- Includes requirements for analyzing and reporting results of controls that are not easily automated
- May require additional data to supplement or clarify security-related information under analysis or provided in initial reports | | Analyze data (3.4.1) | - Security-related information resulting from ISCM is analyzed in the context of stated risk tolerances, potential impact of vulnerabilities on information systems, mission/business processes, and organization as a whole, and potential impact of mitigation options
- Evolving vulnerability and threat data is always considered during analysis
- Organizational officials review analyzed reports to determine whether to conduct mitigation activities or to transfer, avoid/reject, or accept risk
- Authorizing officials may determine accepting some specific risk is preferable to implementing a mitigating response
- Rationale for determinations may include organizational risk tolerance, negative impact to mission/business processes, or cost-effectiveness/return on investment
- Resolution of risk and the rationale for the decision is recorded in accordance with organizational policies and procedures | | Analyze data expected outputs | - Analysis of security status information for all tiers
- Updated System Security Plan, Security Assessment Report, and Plan of Action and Milestones
- Revised organizational risk management decisions | | Report on security control assessments (3.4.2) | - Organizations report on assessments of all implemented security controls for effectiveness in accordance with organizational requirements
- Security-related information from assessments may be conveyed in templates or spreadsheets or collected and reported in an automated fashion
- At the system level, security-related information from assessments directly supports ongoing authorization decisions and plans of action and milestones creation and tracking
- Some security controls or elements of security controls are security metrics (e.g., SI-4 Information System Monitoring), so assessing them results in monitoring the related metric | | Report on security control assessments frequencies/examples | - Risk executive (function) may receive a general report on all systems annually and a detailed report on specific high-impact systems quarterly
- CIO and SISO may receive more granular technical data on all systems quarterly
- AO may receive monthly comprehensive reports on the systems for which s/he is responsible
- CIRT lead may receive exception reports when alerts are generated
- Network administrators may review dashboards showing network activity updated every minute, with summary metrics updated hourly or daily | | Report on security status monitoring (3.4.3) | - Organizations develop procedures for reporting on security status monitoring
- Security status data is derived from monitoring predefined metrics across the organization using output generated by organization-wide tools (often implemented as common controls)
- Organization-wide tools may be part of a specific system or systems, but the security-related information generated may not be system-specific | | Reporting requirements recorded in ISCM strategy | - Specific staff/roles to receive ISCM reports
- Content and format of the reports
- Frequency of reports
- Any tools to be used | | Respond to findings | - Response to findings at all tiers may include risk mitigation, risk acceptance, risk avoidance/rejection, or risk sharing/transfer, in accordance with organizational risk tolerance
- Responses are coordinated with appropriate security management activities such as the security-focused configuration management program | | Tier 1 response | - May result in changes to security policies around organizational governance
- May be constrained by mission/business needs and the limitations of the enterprise architecture (including the human components), immutable governance policies, or other external drivers | | Tier 2 response | - May include requests for additional security-related information, new or modified metrics, changes in mission/business processes, or Tier 3 reporting requirements, and/or additions or modifications to common control implementations
- May be constrained by organizational governance policies and strategies as well as mission/business goals and objectives and limitations of organizational resources and infrastructure | | Tier 3 response | - May include implementation of additional controls, modifications to previously implemented controls, removal of systems’ authorization to operate, changes to the frequency of monitoring, and/or additional or more detailed analysis of security-related information
- System-level mitigations are made within constraints set by Tier 1 and 2 policies, requirements, and strategies | | Response documentation | - Response strategies may be implemented over a period of time, documenting implementation plans in the system’s Plan of Action and Milestones
- As weaknesses are found, response actions are evaluated and any mitigation actions are conducted immediately or are added to the POA&M
- Other key system documents are updated accordingly
- Security controls modified, enhanced, or added as part of response are assessed to ensure new or revised controls are effective in their implementations
- Going forward, new or revised controls are included in the overall continuous monitoring strategy | | Review/update monitoring program and strategy | - ISCM strategies and programs are not static
- Security control assessments, security status metrics, and monitoring and assessment frequencies change in accordance with organizational needs
- Continuous monitoring strategy is reviewed to ensure it supports operating within acceptable risk tolerance levels, metrics remain relevant, and data is current and complete
- The organization establishes a procedure for reviewing and modifying all aspects of the ISCM strategy, including relevance of the overall strategy, accuracy in reflecting organizational risk tolerance, accuracy/correctness of measurements, and applicability of metrics, reporting requirements, and monitoring and assessment frequencies | | Factors precipitating monitoring strategy changes | - Changes to core missions or business processes
- Significant changes in the enterprise architecture (including addition or removal of systems)
- Changes in organizational risk tolerance
- Changes in threat information
- Changes in vulnerability information
- Changes within information systems (including changes in categorization/impact level)
- Increase/decrease in POA&Ms related to specific controls
- Trend analyses of status reporting output
- New federal laws or regulations
- Changes to reporting requirements | | Review/update outputs | - Revised ISCM strategy
- Or a brief documented report noting review details and that modifications to the strategy were not necessary (in accordance with the established review process) | | ISCM strategy review criteria | - Relevance of the overall strategy
- Accuracy in reflecting organizational risk tolerance
- Accuracy/correctness of measurements
- Applicability of metrics
- Reporting requirements
- Monitoring and assessment frequencies | | Monitoring and assessment frequency criteria | - Security control volatility
- System categorizations/impact levels
- Security controls or specific assessment objects providing critical functions
- Security controls with identified weaknesses
- Organizational risk tolerance
- Threat information
- Vulnerability information
- Risk assessment results
- Output of monitoring strategy reviews
- Reporting requirements | | Security control volatility examples | - CM-6 Configuration Settings and CM-8 Information System Component Inventory may require more frequent assessment and monitoring
- PS-2 Position Categorization and PS-3 Personnel Screening typically require less frequent assessment | | Critical function examples | - Log management server
- Firewalls | | Weaknesses and POA&M monitoring | - Existing risks documented in SARs are considered for more frequent monitoring to ensure risks stay within tolerance
- Controls documented in the POA&M as having weaknesses are monitored more frequently until remediation of the weakness is complete
- Minor or low-impact weaknesses are monitored less frequently than higher-impact weaknesses | | Organizational risk tolerance examples | - Low tolerance organizations include those processing, storing, or transmitting large amounts of proprietary and/or personally identifiable information (PII), organizations with numerous high-impact systems, organizations facing specific persistent threats | | Threat information examples | - Known exploits and attack patterns
- Temporary or permanent increases to monitoring frequencies may be used if a specific attack exploits a vulnerability of an implemented technology | | Vulnerability information example | - If a specific product manufacturer provides software patches monthly, an organization might consider vulnerability scans on that product at least that often | | Reporting requirements example | - If OMB policy requires quarterly reports on the number of unauthorized components detected and corrective actions taken, the organization would monitor the system for unauthorized components at least quarterly | | AC-2 example | - AC-2, Account Management, has ten separate requirements (a. through j.) within the base control and four control enhancements [(1) through (4)]
- AC-2a (identification of account types) is a candidate for relatively infrequent assessment
- AC-2h (deactivation of temporary accounts and accounts of terminated or transferred users) would most likely be assessed more frequently than AC-2a
- AC-2 (3) automatically disables accounts after a specified time period of inactivity and is a candidate for relatively frequent monitoring | | Sampling guidance | - Organizations may find collecting data from every object of every system impractical or cost-prohibitive

- Risk: sample population may fail to capture variations in assessment outcomes that would be obtained from full population assessment
- NIST SP 800-53A describes how to achieve satisfactory coverage for examine, interview, and test
- Coverage criteria: types of objects; number of each type; specific objects per type assessed | | Sampling considerations | - Desired information
- Cost and practicality of making the assessment
- Information already known about the objects, organization, or operating environments
- Anticipated variability across the total population

- Supporting Roles: Risk Executive (Function), Authorizing Official, Chief Information Officer, Senior Information Security Officer | | Sampling expected input/output | - Expected Input: Organizational- and system-level policy and procedures on ISCM strategy, metrics, and the Security Assessment Plan updated with assessment and monitoring frequencies
- Expected Output: Security Assessment Plan documentation on acceptable sample sizes, security-related information | | ISCM architecture requirements | - Data collection
- Data storage
- Data analysis capabilities
- Retrieval and presentation (reporting) capabilities | | ISCM architecture characteristics | - Methodologies standardized to facilitate efficiencies, intra- and inter-tier information exchange, correlation, and other analysis

- Interoperable data specifications (e.g., SCAP, XML) enable data to be collected once and reused many times | | Implementation stage data sources | - People

- May require an unplanned assessment of the type defined in the ISCM strategy or a customized assessment tailored to address an emerging need (e.g., a change in planned assessment or monitoring frequency)
- Criteria consider incidents, new threat information, significant changes to systems and operating environments, new or additional mission responsibilities, and results of a security impact analysis (SIA) or assessment of risk
- Depending on significance, an event-driven assessment may trigger one or more system reauthorizations | | Event-driven assessment output | - Documented criteria and thresholds for event-driven assessments/authorizations (e.g., significant change procedures, policy and procedures on event-driven authorizations) | | ISCM roles and responsibilities in process | - Tier 1 and Tier 2 officials provide input to development of the organizational ISCM strategy, including establishment of metrics, policy, procedures, compiling and correlating Tier 3 data into security-related information usable at Tiers 1 and 2, policies on assessment and monitoring frequencies, and provisions for ensuring sufficient depth and coverage when sampling methodologies are utilized
- Review monitoring results to determine security status in accordance with organizational policy and definitions
- Analyze potential security impact to organization and mission/business process functions resulting from changes to information systems and their environments of operation, along with security impact to the enterprise architecture resulting from addition or removal of information systems

- Support planning and implementation of security controls, deployment of automation tools, and how those tools interface with one another in support of the ISCM strategy
- Determine security impact of changes to the information system and its environment of operation, including commissioning or decommissioning the system

content:
### Operational runbook / SOP structure and cadence
- **Chapter Two: The Fundamentals**
  - **2.1 Overview**

  - **2.1.2 The Challenge of Protecting Information and Managing Risk**

  - **2.3.4 Component Inventory**
  - **2.3.5 Configuration Items**
  - **2.3.6 Secure Configurations of Information Systems**
  - **2.3.7 Baseline Configuration**
  - **2.3.8 Configuration Change Control**
  - **2.3.9 Security Impact Analysis**
  - **2.3.10 Configuration Monitoring**
  - **2.4 SecCM Roles and Responsibilities**
- **Chapter Three: The Process**
  - **3.1 Planning**
  - **3.1.1 Planning at the Organizational Level**
  - **3.1.2 Planning at the System Level**
  - **3.2 Identifying and Implementing Configurations**
  - **3.2.1 Establish Secure Configurations**
  - **3.2.2 Implement Secure Configurations**
  - **3.3 Controlling Configuration Change**
  - **3.3.1 Implement Access Restrictions for Change**
  - **3.3.2 Implement the Configuration Change Control Process**
  - **3.3.3 Conduct Security Impact Analysis**
  - **3.3.4 Record and Archive**
  - **3.4 SecCM Monitoring**
  - **3.4.1 Assessment and Reporting**
  - **3.4.2 Implement and Manage Tools for SecCM Monitoring**
  - **3.5 Using Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP)**

### Recurring security / compliance task execution
- **SecCM phases**
  - **Planning**
  - **Identifying and Implementing Configurations**
  - **Controlling Configuration Changes**
  - **Monitoring**
- **Planning phase activities**
  - Develop policy and procedures
  - Disseminate policy throughout the organization
  - Establish a Configuration Control Board (CCB)
  - Create a component inventory
  - Identify configuration items
  - Develop baseline configuration
  - Develop configuration change control process
  - Develop monitoring and reporting process
  - Develop SecCM monitoring strategy
  - Define changes that do not require configuration change control
  - Develop SecCM training
  - Identify approved IT products
  - Identify tools
  - Establish configuration test environment and program
- **System-level planning phase outputs**
  - Completed SecCM Plan
  - Established Configuration Control Board
  - Accurate system component inventory
  - Defined configuration items for the system
- **Identifying and Implementing Configurations**
  - Establish secure configurations
  - Prioritize configurations
  - Test configurations
  - Resolve issues and document deviations
  - Record and approve the baseline configuration
  - Deploy the baseline configuration
- **Controlling Configuration Changes**
  - Implement access restrictions for change
  - Implement configuration change control process
  - Conduct security impact analysis
  - Record and archive
- **Monitoring**
  - Assessment and reporting
  - Implement and manage tools for SecCM monitoring
- **SCAP use**
  - Automate configuration management
  - Produce assessment evidence
  - Automatically verify installation of patches
  - Check system security configuration settings against an expected baseline
  - Examine systems for signs of compromise

### Roles and responsibilities
| Role | Responsibilities explicitly stated |
|---|---|
| **Chief Information Officer (CIO)** | Designates and/or provides a SecCM Program Manager for the organization; approves the organizational SecCM plan and policies. |
| **Senior Agency Information Security Officer (SAISO)** | May act as the SecCM Program Manager for the organization; may provide staff with security expertise to serve on the CCB and/or conduct security impact analyses. |
| **Authorizing Official (AO)** | Manages or participates in the CCB for systems s/he authorizes; may provide technical staff to conduct and/or review security impact analyses; coordinates with the Risk Executive (Function) on SecCM issues; makes final determination whether a given change or set of changes continues to be an acceptable security risk. |
| **System Owner** | Identifies, defines, and ensures implementation of the aspects of SecCM for the information system not defined by the organization; ensures implementation of organizational-level SecCM requirements for the system. |
| **SecCM Program Manager** | Develops SecCM policies and procedures; provides direction; oversees implementation of the SecCM program for the organization and/or system level; facilitates communications; considers dashboard/web site/email/newsletter communications; provides knowledge and direction in policies, procedures, communications, training, defined roles and responsibilities, support, oversight of program activities, and coordination with stakeholders. |
| **System Security Officer (SSO)** | Assists the system owner with implementation of SecCM for the system; conducts configuration monitoring activities (reporting and analysis); may serve on the CCB. |
| **System Administrator (SA)** | Implements agreed-upon secure baseline configurations; incorporates secure configuration settings for IT products; assists with security impact analyses and configuration monitoring activities as needed; may be included in determining baseline configuration for each CI; may serve on the CCB; responsible for complying with SecCM policies and implementing/following SecCM procedures. |
| **System/Software Developer** | Ensures secure configuration settings are built into applications in accordance with security requirements; assists with security impact analyses and configuration monitoring activities as needed; may be included in determining baseline configuration for relevant CIs; may serve on the CCB; responsible for complying with SecCM policies and implementing/following SecCM procedures. |
| **System User (SU)** | Initiates change requests; assists with functional testing; complies with SecCM requirements. |
| **Configuration Control Board (CCB)** | Review and approve changes to an information system; acts as a check and balance on configuration change activity; ensures changes are held to organizationally defined criteria before implementation; gatekeeper for changes introduced into a system. |

### CCB / escalation / exception handling / decisioning
- **CCB**
  - Typically consists of **two or more individuals**
  - Represents various perspectives from within the organization
  - May be less formal for systems with limited size, scope, and criticality
  - Organization determines size and formality appropriate for a given system or systems
  - Establishment is part of the Planning phase
  - Supports **CM-3 Configuration Change Control**
- **CCB charter**
  - May define:
    - Membership
    - Roles and responsibilities of members
    - Reporting relationship to oversight body like an **Executive Steering Committee** or the **Risk Executive (Function)**
    - How the CCB operates
    - How to handle changes
    - Range of dispositions: **approved, not approved, on hold, etc.**
    - Evaluation criteria
    - Quorum required to make configuration change control-related decisions
- **CCB size/formality**
  - Low-impact and/or small, uncomplicated systems: CCB may be composed of as few as **two members** (typically the system owner and the SSO)
  - High-impact systems and complex moderate-impact systems: CCB may be composed of at least **three individuals**, at least one of whom is a system owner or SSO
- **Decision escalation / risk acceptance**
  - AO coordinates with the Risk Executive (Function) on SecCM issues
  - AO makes final determination whether a given change or set of changes continues to be an acceptable security risk
  - If change is significant enough that system authorization is in question, meet with AO and System Owner to determine if re-authorization is necessary; **CCB or RE(F) may also be involved**
- **Exception / unscheduled / unauthorized changes**
  - Some changes may be **preapproved** or **exempt from configuration control**
  - If exempt or pre-approved, note this on the change request and allow the change to be made without further analysis or approval
  - System documentation may still require updating
  - Unscheduled changes are still managed and controlled
  - Instructions for handling unscheduled changes and unauthorized changes discovered later are included in configuration change control procedures
  - Unscheduled changes are reviewed/resolved by the CCB as soon as is practical after they are made
  - Requirements for retroactive analysis, testing, and approval of changes implemented outside of the change control process are included in procedures
- **Approval / escalation criteria**
  - Criteria for changes that are preapproved or exempt from configuration control
  - Criteria to determine whether a change is significant enough to trigger consideration of system reauthorization activities
  - Criteria for elevating a change request from system level approval to organizational approval
  - Requirements for rollback of changes
  - Requirements for management of unscheduled changes tailored to support expedited reviews and approvals

### Cadence / frequencies / schedules
- **SecCM monitoring strategy**
  - Includes a **schedule** for SecCM monitoring and associated reporting
  - Includes **scheduled and ad hoc assessments**
  - Monitoring schedule may coincide with scheduled releases such that assessments are performed **before and after deployments**
  - Schedule includes provisions for reviewing and revising the SecCM monitoring strategy
- **CCB charter sample**
  - State the **frequency of regularly scheduled CCB meetings**
  - State the conditions that trigger a **special meeting**
- **SecCM policy**
  - Policies are **periodically reviewed and updated**
- **Monitoring strategy**
  - Strategy and procedures are **reviewed and revised** to ensure organizational security requirements continue to be met
- **Tools**
  - If automated tools are used for component inventory, procedures may describe **how often they will run**
- **Tests**
  - Configuration test environment used for testing IT products, tools, and proposed changes prior to rollout
  - Virtual environments are recommended for testing secure configurations
  - Monitoring can coincide with release cycles

### Audit evidence / artifacts / records
- **SecCM policy records**
  - Records of configuration management activities to be maintained
  - Information to be included in each type of record
  - Who is responsible for writing/keeping the records
  - Procedures for protecting, accessing, auditing, and ultimately deleting such records
- **Artifacts explicitly named**
  - Configuration Management Plan
  - SecCM Plan
  - Change requests
  - Approvals
  - Security impact analyses
  - Reporting on SecCM
  - CCB minutes
  - Actions to be taken
  - Assigned responsibilities for actions
  - Reports generated
  - Approvals/disapprovals and rationale
  - System Security Plans
  - Security Assessment Reports
  - Security Status Reports
  - Risk Assessments
  - Plans of Action & Milestones
  - Technical designs
  - Baseline configurations
  - Component inventory
  - Configuration change control records
  - Audit records
  - Inventory reports
  - Monitoring reports
  - Security assessment reports
  - Output from automated tools
  - Media library records
  - Archived baseline configurations
- **Security impact analysis / monitoring evidence**
  - Evidence can be produced automatically by SCAP-enabled tools
  - SCAP-expressed checklists can automatically generate standardized assessment and compliance evidence
  - Monitoring reports can support metrics and continuous monitoring requirements
  - Results of monitoring are reported to management
  - Archived baseline configurations are useful for incident response and traceability support during formal audits
- **Configuration change control evidence**
  - Record the change request
  - Document security impact analysis findings
  - Document testing results
  - Document implemented changes to baseline
  - Retain several iterations of baselines for audit, incident response, and historical purposes
- **Configuration monitoring evidence**
  - Systems inconsistent with baseline configuration
  - Unapproved components
  - Disparities between approved baseline and actual configuration
  - Querying audit records/log monitoring to identify unauthorized change events
  - Reviewing configuration change control records including security impact analyses
  - Reports used as input to RMF continuous monitoring
- **Media library**
  - Stores, protects, and controls all authorized versions of media CIs
  - May include commercially licensed software, custom-developed software, and other artifacts and documents generated throughout the SDLC

### Templates / forms / headings
- **Appendix D: Sample Outline for a Security Configuration Management Plan**
  - **1. INTRODUCTION**
    - **1.1 BACKGROUND**
    - **1.2 OVERVIEW OF SYSTEM**
      - **1.2.1 System Mission**
      - **1.2.2 Data Flow Description**
      - **1.2.3 System Architecture**
      - **1.2.4 System Administration and Management Activities**
    - **1.3 PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT**
    - **1.4 SCOPE**
    - **1.5 APPLICABLE POLICIES AND PROCEDURES**
  - **2. SecCM PROGRAM**
    - **2.1 SecCM ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES**
    - **2.2 SecCM PROGRAM ADMINISTRATION**
      - **2.2.1 SecCM Policies and Procedures (included herein or by reference)**
      - **2.2.2 Configuration Control Board Functions**
      - **2.2.3 Establishment of Change Control Board at the Organization Level**
      - **2.2.4 Establishment of Change Control Board at the System Level**
      - **2.2.5 Schedules and Resource Requirements**
    - **2.3 SecCM TOOLS**
      - **2.3.1 SCM Tools**
      - **2.3.2 SCM Library**
    - **2.4 SecCM RETENTION, ARCHIVING, STORAGE AND DISPOSAL**
  - **3. SecCM ACTIVITIES**
    - **3.1 CONFIGURATION IDENTIFICATION**
      - **3.1.1 Types of Configuration Items (CI)**
      - **3.1.2 Identification Criteria**
      - **3.1.3 Configuration Item Labeling**
    - **3.2 CONFIGURATION BASELINING**
      - **3.2.1 Identification of Applicable Common Secure Configurations**
      - **3.2.2 Information System Component CI Baselines**
      - **3.2.3 Non-Component Object CI Baselines**
    - **3.3 CONFIGURATION CHANGE CONTROL**
      - **3.3.1 Handling of Scheduled, Unscheduled, and Unauthorized Changes**
      - **3.3.2 Security Impact Analysis**
      - **3.3.3 Testing**
      - **3.3.4 Submission of Findings to the Change Control Board**
      - **3.3.5 Change Control Board Evaluation and Approval Process**
      - **3.3.6 Recording Requirements**
    - **3.4 SecCM MONITORING**
      - **3.4.1 Organization Level Tools**
      - **3.4.2 System Level Tools**
      - **3.4.3 Monitoring Requirements and Frequencies**
    - **3.5 SecCM REPORTING**
      - **3.5.1 Report Recipients**
      - **3.5.2 Reviewing Reports**
  - **Potential SecCM Plan Appendices**
    - **CCB Charter**
    - **Change Request Form Template**
    - **Security Impact Analysis Report Format**
    - **References**
- **Appendix E: Sample Change Request**
  - **1. Date Prepared**
  - **2. Title of Change Request**
  - **3. Change Initiator/Project Manager**
  - **4. Change Description**
  - **5. Change Justification**
  - **6. Urgency of Change: {Scheduled/Urgent/Unscheduled}**
  - **7. System Components/CIs to be Changed**
  - **8. Other System Components, CIs, or Systems to Be Affected by Change**
  - **9. Personnel involved with the Change**
  - **10. Expected Security Impact of Change**
  - **11. Expected Functional Impact of Change**
  - **12. Expected Impact of Not Doing Change**
  - **13. Potential Interface/Integration Issues**
  - **14. Required Changes to Existing Applications**
  - **15. Project work plan including change implementation date, deliverables, and back-out plan**
  - **16. Funding Required to Implement Change**
  - **Change Approved/Disapproved (include justification and/or further action to be taken if disapproved)**
  - **Authorized Signature(s)**
  - **NOTE: Supporting documentation may be attached to the Change Request.**
- **Appendix H: CCB Charter Sample**
  - **PURPOSE**
  - **SCOPE OF AUTHORITY**
  - **MEMBERSHIP**
  - **OPERATING PROCEDURES**
  - **DECISION-MAKING PROCESS**
  - **COMMUNICATING STATUS**
- **Appendix I: Sample Security Impact Analysis Template**
  - **Table 1: Initiative/Release Background**
  - **Table 2: Initiative/Release Description and Potential Security Issues**
  - **Table 3: Change Type Worksheet**
  - **Table 4: Device Impact Worksheet**
  - **Table 5: Testing Worksheet**
  - **Table 6: Analysis Worksheet**
  - **ATTACHMENT I: SECURITY IMPACT WORKSHEET**

### Table: Appendix I captured fields
| Table | Fields / headings explicitly stated |
|---|---|
| **Table 1: Initiative/Release Background** | Initiative/Release Name; Project Type; System Changes; Baseline Changes; Security Risks; Planned Deployment Initiation Date; Planned Deployment Completion Date; System(s) Impacted by change; Current Security Categorization of Impacted System(s); [Insert initiative/release background info required by the organization as applicable] |
| **Table 2: Initiative/Release Description and Potential Security Issues** | What are the business requirements driving the change?; Please provide a description of the proposed change(s), including ALL additions, deletions, and modifications.; Is the Technical Lead and/or Project Lead aware of any potential security-related issues or challenges associated with this change? If so, briefly describe them or provide and attachment describing them. |
| **Table 3: Change Type Worksheet** | Change Type; Applicable? (Mark X if Applicable); Explanation (If Applicable); New network device(s) (e.g., router, switch, firewall, VPN gateway); New server(s); New workstation(s) (desktops or laptops); Other new HW; Decommissioning of existing HW; New virtual server; New OS; Upgrade of existing OS; New COTS application; Upgrade or patch of COTS application; New custom application; Upgrade or bug fix for existing custom application; New DBMS (e.g., Microsoft SQL Server or Oracle); Upgrade of existing DBMS (e.g., Oracle 9i to 10g); Addition of new DB instance; Modification of an existing DB instance (e.g., changes to a table); New or upgraded Middleware application or service; Modifications to ports, protocols, and services used or provided by the system; Changes intended to address security requirements or improve/modify the security of the system (e.g., cryptographic modules, security patch, authentication, authorization, role changes); New information type processed, stored, or transmitted on the system; Interface change (addition/removed); Change of location; Other change |
| **Table 4: Device Impact Worksheet** | System Name; Device Name; IP Address; Manufacturer; Model; Serial No.; Asset/Component Property ID; OS; Software Description |
| **Table 5: Testing Worksheet** | Please describe the tests that were conducted against the change?; Please provide a description of the test results for each change (or provide reference to another document with test results). |
| **Table 6: Analysis Worksheet** | Analysis, Recommendations, and Requirements; [Reviewed by: Name (Title)]; Signature; [Insert relevant role]; [Date] |

### File / appendix-specific fields and controls
- **Organizational SecCM policy includes**
  - Purpose
  - Scope
  - Roles
  - Responsibilities
  - Activities
  - Common secure configurations
  - Records
- **SecCM procedures address**
  - Templates
  - Component Inventory
  - Baseline Configuration
  - Common Secure Configurations
  - Patch Management
  - Configuration Change Control
  - Help Desk Procedures
  - SDLC Procedures
  - Monitoring
  - Media Library Procedures
- **Component inventory data elements explicitly listed**
  - Unique Identifier and/or Serial Number
  - System of which the component is a part
  - Type of component
  - Manufacturer/Model information
  - Operating System Type and Version/Service Pack Level
  - Presence of virtual machines
  - Application Software Version/License information
  - Physical location
  - Logical location
  - Media Access Control (MAC) address
  - Owner
  - Operational status
  - Primary and secondary administrators
  - Primary user
  - Status of the component
  - Relationships to other system components in the inventory
  - Relationships to/dependencies on other systems
  - Other systems supported by this component
  - Identification of any Service-Level Agreements (SLA) that apply to the component
  - Applicable common secure configurations
  - Configuration item (CI) of which it is a part
  - Controls supported by this component
  - Identification of any incident logs that apply to the component
- **Configuration item data elements explicitly listed**
  - The system of which the CI is a part
  - Logical and/or physical placement within the system
  - Ownership and management information
  - Inventory of system components that makes up the CI
  - Inventory of documentation that makes up the CI
  - Version numbers for components and non-component objects
  - Relationship to/dependencies on other CIs within the system
  - Information related to custom software used within the CI
  - IT products or components common secure configurations
  - Any other information needed to rebuild or reconstitute the CI
- **SCAP-enabled evidence / components**
  - Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format (XCCDF) 1.2
  - Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) 5.11.2
  - Open Checklist Interactive Language (OCIL) 2.0
  - Asset Reporting Format (ARF) 1.1
  - Asset Identification 1.1
  - Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) 2.3
  - Software Identification (SWID) Tags 2015
  - Common Configuration Enumeration (CCE) 5
  - Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)
  - Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 3
  - Common Configuration Scoring System (CCSS) 1.0
  - Trust Model for Security Automation Data (TMSAD) 1.0
- **Automation / reporting requirements**
  - At minimum, organizations consider tools that can automatically assess configuration settings of system components
  - Select automated tools that can scan different system components running different operating systems, identify current configuration settings, and indicate where current settings are noncompliant with policy
  - Tools may integrate with help desk, inventory management, incident response, SIEM, dashboard products
  - Standardized reporting capability including ability to tailor output and drill down
  - Data consolidation into SIEM tools and dashboard products
  - Automated tools can facilitate reporting for Security Information and Event Management applications
  - Normalize data to combine, correlate, analyze, and report monitoring outputs consistently

### Fields captured in monitoring / analysis / reporting
- **Monitoring reconciliation questions**
  - Who made the change
  - Whether the change occurred in a scheduled maintenance window
  - Whether the change matches a previously detected and approved change
  - Whether the change corresponds with an approved change request, help desk ticket, or product release
- **Monitoring metrics examples**
  - Percentage of systems implemented in accordance with approved baselines
  - Percentage of IT products configured in accordance with organizationally defined common secure configurations
  - Percentage of system changes subjected to security impact analyses
- **Security impact analysis worksheet questions**
  - AC
  - AT
  - AU
  - CM
  - IA
  - MA
  - MP
  - PE
  - SC
  - SI

### Security / compliance task execution specifics
- **Secure configuration establishment may include**
  - Secure values for OS and application features
  - Services and ports
  - Network protocols and network interfaces
  - Methods of remote access
  - Access controls
  - Management of identifiers/accounts
  - Authentication controls
  - Audit settings
  - System settings
  - Cryptography using [FIPS 140-3]-validated cryptographic protocols and algorithms
  - Vendor-released patches in response to vulnerabilities
  - Approved, signed software, if supported
  - Safeguards through software for endpoint machines
  - Network protections
  - Physical/logical location of component
  - Maintaining technical specification and design documentation, system security documentation, system procedures
- **Configuration change control steps**
  - Request the change
  - Record the request for the proposed change
  - Determine if the proposed change requires configuration control
  - Analyze the proposed change for its security impact on the system
  - Test the proposed change for security and functional impacts
  - Approve the change
  - Implement the approved change
  - Verify that the change was implemented correctly
  - Close out the change request
- **Security impact analysis steps**
  - Understand the change
  - Identify vulnerabilities
  - Assess risks
  - Assess impact on existing security controls
  - Plan safeguards and countermeasures
- **Monitoring activities**
  - Scanning to discover components not recorded in the inventory
  - Scanning to identify disparities between the approved baseline configuration and the actual configuration for a system
  - Implementation of automated change monitoring tools
  - Querying audit records/log monitoring to identify unauthorized change events
  - Running system integrity checks
  - Reviewing configuration change control records including security impact analyses
  - Taking remedial action such as quarantining unregistered device(s), blocking insecure protocols, sending alerts, rolling back changes, restoring from backups, updating inventory, updating baseline configurations

### Notifications / communication
- **SecCM Program Manager**
  - Facilitates communications regarding SecCM policies, procedures, issues, etc., within the organization
  - Considers security information management console or “dashboard”
  - Considers Web site updates, emails, and newsletters
- **CCB sample charter “COMMUNICATING STATUS”**
  - Communicate each decision to:
    - the individual who requested the change
    - senior management
    - project management
    - affected team members who must implement the change
    - higher- or lower-level CCBs
    - any other stakeholders
  - Indicate where decisions and supporting information, rationale, or data will be stored

### Absence notes
- **No SLAs, severity bands, or response-time SLAs** are stated for operational handling.
- **No ticket workflow system names** are stated beyond help desk, email, paper-based requests, and automated tools.
- **No explicit remediation POA&M workflow** is defined beyond Plans of Action & Milestones being updated in record-and-archive activities.

title: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning: - NIST
content:
- **Document**
  - **NIST SP 800-40r4**
  - **Title:** *Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning: Preventive Maintenance for Technology*
  - **Date:** **April 2022**

- **Purpose and scope**
  - Help organizations improve **enterprise patch management planning** to strengthen **management of risk**.
  - Treat enterprise patch management as **preventive maintenance for an organization’s technology**.
  - Applies to all types of computing technology assets, including:
    - **IT**
    - **operational technology (OT)**
    - **Internet of Things (IoT)**
    - **mobile devices**
    - **cloud computing**
  - Applies to all types of patchable software, including:
    - **applications**
    - **operating systems**
    - **firmware**
  - Notes that patch management technologies are minimally discussed; **NIST SP 1800-31** provides information on technologies to implement IT patch management policies and processes.

- **Enterprise patch management definition**
  - Enterprise patch management is the process of:
    - **identifying**
    - **prioritizing**
    - **acquiring**
    - **installing**
    - **verifying the installation**
  - Applies to:
    - **patches**
    - **updates**
    - **upgrades**
  - Throughout an organization.

- **Audience**
  - Primary audience:
    - **chief information officers**
    - **chief information security officers**
    - **cybersecurity directors and managers**
    - others responsible for managing organizational risk related to the use of software
  - Other audiences:
    - business and mission owners
    - security engineers and architects
    - system administrators
    - security operations personnel

- **Publication structure**
  - **Section 2**: risk response approaches for software vulnerabilities and overview of enterprise patch management life cycle
  - **Section 3**: principles and actionable recommendations for enterprise patch management planning
  - **References**
  - **Appendix A**: NIST Cybersecurity Framework Subcategories and SP 800-53 controls most important for enterprise patch management policies and processes
  - **Appendix B**: acronym list

- **Risk responses**
  - Four types of risk responses:
    1. **Accept**
       - Accept the risk from vulnerable software as is
       - Examples:
         - rely on existing security controls to prevent vulnerability exploitation
         - determine the potential impact is low enough that no additional action is needed
    2. **Mitigate**
       - Reduce the risk by:
         - eliminating vulnerabilities
         - deploying additional security controls to reduce vulnerability exploitation
       - Examples:
         - patching vulnerable software
         - disabling a vulnerable feature
         - upgrading to a newer software version without the vulnerabilities
         - using firewalls and network segmentation to isolate vulnerable assets
    3. **Transfer**
       - Reduce the risk by sharing some consequences with another party
       - Examples:
         - purchasing cybersecurity insurance
         - replacing conventional software installations with **software-as-a-service (SaaS)** where the vendor/managed service provider takes care of patching
    4. **Avoid**
       - Ensure the risk does not occur by eliminating the attack surface
       - Examples:
         - uninstalling the vulnerable software
         - decommissioning assets with the vulnerabilities
         - disabling computing capabilities in assets that can function without them

- **Why immediate patching may not be viable**
  - Patch may not be available yet
  - Vendor may no longer support the vulnerable software
  - Need to wait for a scheduled outage window
  - Need to perform testing first
  - Need to update other software that interacts with the software to be patched
  - Need to train employees on new features or interfaces
  - Some patches may be a higher priority, so other patches are delayed due to limited resources
  - Manufacturer may require delayed schedule for assets with human safety implications in a highly regulated sector because extensive testing and certification must be performed first
  - In some cases, organizations implementing updates on their own may be voiding the product warranty and preventing future support from the manufacturer
  - Need to comply with specific legal, regulatory, or business requirements
  - Example: need **FIPS-validated cryptographic modules** for protecting data, but the upgraded software’s cryptographic modules are not yet FIPS-validated

- **Software vulnerability management life cycle**
  - Applies to all risk response approaches
  - Steps:
    1. **Know when new software vulnerabilities affect your organization’s assets**
       - Includes applications, operating systems, and firmware
       - Know what assets the organization uses and which software and software versions those assets run
       - Track down to the level of **packages and libraries**
       - Keep track of new vulnerabilities in that software
       - Example sources:
         - vulnerability feeds from software vendors
         - security researchers
         - **National Vulnerability Database (NVD)**
    2. **Plan the risk response**
       - Assess the risk the vulnerability poses
       - Choose which form of risk response, or combination of forms, to use
       - Decide how to implement the risk response
       - Example:
         - determine risk is elevated because the vulnerability is present in many organization assets and is being exploited in the wild
         - choose mitigation
         - mitigate by upgrading vulnerable software and altering configuration settings
    3. **Execute the risk response**
       - Common phases:
         a. Prepare the risk response
         b. Implement the risk response
         c. Verify the risk response
         d. Continuously monitor the risk response
  - Administrative activities throughout the life cycle:
    - updating documentation
    - audit logging
    - generating actionable insights and reports as part of enterprise change management
  - Robust change management policies and processes are described as fundamental

- **Risk response execution phases**
  - **Prepare to deploy the patch**
    - Prioritize the patch
    - Schedule patch deployment
    - Acquire the patch
    - Validate the patch
    - Test the patch
  - **Deploy the patch**
    - Distribute the patch
    - Validate the patch
    - Install the patch
    - Change software configuration and state
    - Resolve any issues
  - **Verify deployment**
    - Ensure the patch has been installed successfully and taken effect
    - Automated means are generally needed to achieve verification at scale
  - **Monitor the deployed patches**
    - Confirm the patch is still installed
    - Verify the patch has not been uninstalled by a user or an attacker
    - Verify an unpatched version has not been restored from a backup
    - Verify the device has not been reset to a vulnerable factory-default state
    - Monitor for behavior changes after patching
    - May help detect/respond/recover if the installed patch was itself compromised

- **Prepare to deploy the patch — common steps**
  - **Prioritize the patch**
    - Higher priority if deployment would reduce cybersecurity risk more than other patches
    - Lower priority if it addresses a low-risk vulnerability on a small number of low-importance assets
  - **Schedule patch deployment**
    - Many organizations schedule patch deployments as part of enterprise change management activities
  - **Acquire the patch**
    - Downloaded from the internet
    - Built internally by developers or system administrators
    - Provided through removable media
  - **Validate the patch**
    - Authenticity and integrity should be confirmed
    - Preferably by automated means
    - Before the patch is tested or installed
  - **Test the patch**
    - May be tested before deployment
    - Intended to reduce operational risk by identifying problems before production
    - Testing may be manual or automated

- **Deploy the patch — factors affecting deployment**
  - Type of software being updated:
    - firmware
    - operating system (OS)
    - application
  - Asset platform type:
    - IT
    - OT
    - IoT
    - mobile
    - cloud
    - virtual machine (VM)
    - containers
  - Platform traits:
    - managed/unmanaged asset
    - on-premises or not
    - virtualized or not
    - containerized or not
  - Environmental limitations:
    - network connectivity
    - bandwidth

- **Deploy the patch — common steps**
  - **Distribute the patch**
    - Organization-controlled:
      - automatically
      - manually
      - as scheduled
    - Vendor-controlled:
      - delivered from the cloud
  - **Validate the patch**
    - Confirm authenticity and integrity before installation
    - Preferably through automated means
  - **Install the patch**
    - Automatically
    - Manually when directed by a user, administrator, vendor, or tool
    - As a result of other software being installed or updated
    - Through replacement of removable media used by an asset
    - Some installations require administrator privileges
      - Example: firmware patches for a system basic input/output system (**BIOS**)
    - Some installations require user participation or cooperation
  - **Change software configuration and state**
    - Examples:
      - restarting patched software
      - rebooting the operating system or platform
      - redeploying applications
      - altering software configuration settings
    - In other cases, no such changes are needed
  - **Resolve any issues**
    - Side effects may:
      - alter existing security configuration settings
      - add new settings
      - create a new security problem while fixing the original one
    - Operational issues may require:
      - uninstalling the patch
      - reverting to the previous version
      - restoring software or asset from backups

- **Recommendations for enterprise patch management planning**
  - Principles:
    - **Problems are inevitable; be prepared for them**
    - **Simplify decision making**
    - **Rely on automation**
    - **Start improvements now**
  - Patch management challenges noted:
    - trade-off between earlier deployment and more testing
    - patches more quickly reduce attacker window but increase operational disruption risk
    - testing decreases disruption risk but increases attacker window
    - testing can consume considerable staff resources and still miss problems
    - dynamic and dispersed computing assets
    - large number of installed software components
    - different processes/technology by asset type:
      - OT
      - IoT
      - mobile
      - cloud
      - traditional IT
      - virtual machines
      - containers
    - many organizations are unable to keep up with patching
    - patching often becomes reactive rather than proactive

- **Reduce patching-related disruptions**
  - Decrease the number of vulnerabilities introduced into environments
  - Methods:
    - **Harden software**
      - enforce least privilege
      - enforce least functionality
      - deactivate or uninstall software services, features, and other components not needed
      - reference: *Security Measures for “EO-Critical Software” Use Under Executive Order (EO) 14028 (July 9, 2021)*
    - Acquire software likely to have fewer vulnerabilities over time
    - Work with software development partners likely to introduce fewer vulnerabilities over time
      - consider:
        - rigor of secure software development practices
        - how quickly issues are addressed and patches released
        - how often problems are associated with their patches
        - transparency in security-related communications
    - Use managed services instead of software when feasible
    - Select stacks or platforms likely to have fewer vulnerabilities over time
      - example: running software within a small container instead of a larger operating system
    - Run applications on stacks/platforms where patching is a fundamental part of the deployed technology and is less likely to disrupt operations
      - example: modernizing and running software within cloud-based containers instead of on-premises server operating systems
    - Take advantage of existing toolchains that already build applications with updated components and test them before production release

- **Inventory your software and assets**
  - Establish and constantly maintain up-to-date software inventories for physical and virtual computing assets, including:
    - OT
    - IoT
    - container assets
  - Inventory may be in a single enterprise asset inventory or split among multiple resources
  - A comprehensive inventory is ideal but may be impossible
  - Goal: maintain a close-to-comprehensive inventory by relying on automation to:
    - constantly discover new assets
    - collect up-to-date information on all assets
  - Vendors may provide machine-consumable data on asset software composition, such as **software bill of materials (SBOM)**, to augment inventories
  - Without constant updates, inventories become outdated and inaccurate
  - Monthly or quarterly inventory updates by vulnerability scan are described as a model that should no longer be used
  - Inventory automation techniques and tools:
    - leverage inventory capabilities built into platforms and assets whenever feasible
    - APIs built into cloud-based platforms may enable continuous updates
    - vulnerability scans and passive network monitoring on local networks can contribute to asset inventories, especially discovery
    - if vulnerability scans are used for inventories, authenticated scanning is needed to detect changes
  - Patching should be approached from a per-asset perspective
  - Software inventories should include each computing asset’s:
    - technical characteristics
    - mission/business characteristics
  - Decisions for risk responses and priorities should not be based solely on software and software versions

- **Characteristics to inventory**
  - Technical characteristics:
    - asset’s platform type
      - IT
      - OT
      - IoT
      - mobile
      - cloud
      - VM
    - party who administrates the asset
      - IT department
      - third party
      - end user
      - vendor/manufacturer
      - shared responsibility model
    - applications, services, or other mechanisms used to manage the asset
      - endpoint management software
      - virtual machine manager
      - container management software
    - asset’s network connectivity in terms of:
      - protocols
      - frequency/duration
      - bandwidth
    - technical security controls already in place to safeguard the asset
    - primary user(s) or interconnected services and their privileges
  - Mission/business characteristics:
    - asset’s role and importance to the organization
    - laws, regulations, or policies that specify how soon a new vulnerability in the asset must be addressed
    - contractual restrictions on patching
      - example: highly regulated asset can only be patched by its manufacturer after testing and certification
    - mission/business restrictions on risk responses for that asset
      - example: asset can only be rebooted during a monthly maintenance outage
  - Tracking these characteristics supports:
    - better decision making regarding risk responses and priorities
    - zero-trust architecture efforts
    - incident response investigations if patching history is tracked

- **Define risk response scenarios**
  - Scenarios:
    - **Routine patching**
      - standard procedure for patches on a regular release cycle not elevated to emergency status
      - most patching falls under this scenario
