title: Meeting IRS Safeguards audit requirements
content:
- **Document / source**
  - **Page title:** Meeting IRS Safeguards audit requirements
  - **Source:** IRS Publication 1075, Tax Information Security Guidelines for Federal, State and Local Agencies and Entities
  - **Referenced sections:** section 5.6.2; exhibit 9
  - **Purpose stated:** provide a scenario based technical assistance memo to assist agencies in better understanding and implementing audit based requirements for Safeguards

- **Audit trail / audit log definition and required contents**
  - Audit trail or audit log is a chronological sequence of audit records (audit events)
  - Each audit record contains evidence directly pertaining to and resulting from the execution of a business process or system function
  - Audit records should be generated when subjects perform business related activities with system resources
  - Audit records should also be produced when adversaries try to perform unauthorized activities on the system resources
  - Each audit record captures details related to the underlying event:
    - Date and time of the event
    - Unique ID of the user
    - Type of event
    - Success or failure of event
    - Origin of the request
    - Name of the object introduced/deleted
    - Description of modification to security databases
  - Audit trail should be comprehensive enough to historically recreate the sequence of events leading to successful and unsuccessful access attempts to FTI
  - Questions the audit trail should help answer:
    - Has an unauthorized access to FTI occurred?
    - Was that particular user authorized to have access to FTI?
    - Did they have a need-to-know at the time to gain access to FTI?
    - Was the FTI altered in any way?
    - Did the FTI leave the system?
    - Was FTI disclosed?

- **Exhibit 9 audit trail capture requirements**
  1. All successful login and logoff attempts
  2. All unsuccessful login and authorization attempts
  3. All identification and authentication attempts
  4. All actions, connections and requests performed by privileged users
     - privileged user definition included in page:
       - a user who, by virtue of function, and/or seniority, has been allocated powers within the computer system, which are significantly greater than those available to the majority of users
       - includes, for example, the system administrator(s) and network administrator(s)
       - responsible for keeping the system available
       - may need powers to create new user profiles as well as add to or amend the powers and access rights of existing users
  5. All actions, connections and requests performed by privileged functions
  6. All changes to logical access control authorities (e.g., rights, permissions)
  7. All system changes with the potential to compromise the integrity of audit policy configurations, security policy configurations and audit record generation services
  8. Creation, modification and deletion of objects including files, directories and user accounts
  9. Creation, modification and deletion of user accounts and group accounts
  10. Creation, modification and deletion of user account and group account privileges
  11. Capture:
      - the date of the system event
      - the time of the system event
      - the type of system event initiated
      - the user account, system account, service or process responsible for initiating the system event
  12. System start-up and shutdown functions
  13. Modifications to administrator account(s) and administrator group account(s) including:
      - escalation of user account privileges commensurate with administrator-equivalent account(s)
      - adding or deleting users from the administrator group account(s)
  14. Enabling or disabling of audit report generation services
  15. Command line changes, batch file changes and queries made to the system (e.g., operating system, application, and database)
  16. Audit trail must be protected from unauthorized access, use, deletion or modification
  17. Audit trail must be restricted to personnel routinely responsible for performing security audit functions

- **Agency audit areas to address**
  1. Audit and accountability policy and procedures must be developed, documented, disseminated, and updated
  2. Auditable events must be identified and captured
  3. Content of audit records should be understood and defined
  4. Proper audit storage capacity must be determined and allocated
  5. Audit logs must be reviewed periodically as defined by the policy
  6. Processes must be in place to handle auditing failures
  7. Audit logs must be monitored, analyzed and reporting
  8. Time stamps must be enforced to be able to correlate events from multiple sources
  9. The audit information is sensitive and must be protected
  10. Audit information shall be retained for 6 years

- **Operational guidance / cadence / workflow**
  - Audit capabilities exist at operating system, application, and database level
  - In most cases, auditing at a single layer will not capture the 17 items offered as guidance by Exhibit 9
  - Agencies should examine the layer closest to the FTI data
  - Example:
    - if FTI is stored in a database, audit everything at the table and/or record level in the database that contains FTI
    - log system access events e.g., log-in / log-out at the OS level
    - if FTI is stored in flat files and an application uses the FTI flat data files, audit within the application if it can capture read/update activity
    - if application is not used or does not offer granular enough auditing, leverage operating system auditing capabilities
  - Collecting all audit data is only half the battle
  - Audit data should be monitored, analyzed, protected and retained
  - Policies and procedures should be in place along with collection and correlation of audit logs from all systems that receive, process, store or transmit FTI
  - Policies should clearly define the “who, what, where, when and why” with respect to audit logs
  - Policies should address all requirements for auditing
  - Policies often describe the “what” but neglect the “who” and the process by which logs are monitored, reviewed, protected and retained
  - Expected in policy and procedures:
    - some kind of schedule for reviewing particular audit logs
    - process and workflow for dealing with violations and anomalous activities
    - a quick report even in the form of an email to management whenever these activities occur
  - “One of the most common findings” is not having a comprehensive audit policy and associated procedures implemented to ensure the system audits activities, generates audit reports, and archives audit data

- **Audit log review schedule example**
  
  | Audit Log Review | Roles | Frequency | Violations / Changes to Review |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Audit Log - Daily Review | RACF System Administrator | Daily | Data set access violations; Resource access violations; Program use violations |
  | Audit Log - Weekly/Monthly Review | RACF System Administrator & RACF SA Manager | Weekly/Monthly | Failed logon attempts – RACF user violation report; Special and operation privileges |
  | Audit Log - Quarterly Review | RACF Auditor team | Quarterly | Trusted STC accesses; FTP userids/logonids/ACIDs accesses; Global Control Options |

- **Named roles / responsibilities**
  - RACF System Administrator
  - RACF SA Manager
  - RACF Auditor team
  - system administrator(s)
  - network administrator(s)
  - personnel routinely responsible for performing security audit functions
  - management
  - agency
  - operating system, database, and application vendors (vendor-provided configuration guidance referenced)
  - IRS Safeguards Computer Security Evaluation Matrix (SCSEM) referenced for a particular technology

- **Evidence / artifacts explicitly mentioned**
  - audit logs
  - audit reports
  - archived audit data
  - email to management whenever violations or anomalous activities occur
  - vendor-provided configuration guidance
  - IRS Safeguards Computer Security Evaluation Matrix (SCSEM)
  - Security log in Event Viewer
  - RACF user violation report
  - syslog messages
  - NTP authentication keys
  - SMF audit logs
  - SMF audit files
  - router log files
  - log server
  - access control list associated with SYS1.MAN* (denoted by SYS1.* high-level qualifier)

- **Mainframe - RACF**
  
  | Finding | Discussion | Risk | Recommendation |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | RACF AUDIT operand is not in effect | Analysis of the SETROPTS global settings resource classes are not defined to the AUDIT operand. When enabled, the AUDIT operand ensures RACF logs (1) all changes to resource profiles (RACDEF) and (2) all uses of supervisor calls (SVC) and/or System Authorization Facility (SAF) calls requesting access to specified resources (RACROUTE REQUEST). | If the AUDIT operand is not enabled, RACF will not log (1) all changes to resource profiles, and (2) supervisor calls requesting access to resources. Consequently, unauthorized access to the system and FTI could occur without detection. | Enable the SETROPTS AUDIT operand for all active resource classes used to ensure RACF logs: (1) all changes to resource profiles; and (2) all uses of supervisor calls or SAF calls requesting access to specified resources. In effect the active and audit list of classes should be identical. |
  | STATISTICS processing is not in effect | Analysis of the SETROPTS global settings found the STATISTICS parameter set to NONE. STATISTICS processing records access to resources in specific classes that are protected by discrete profiles. The STATISTICS option permits an installation to record statistics on discrete profiles to see how their respective data sets and resources within specific resource classes are being used. Specific resources with unique security concerns, such as those with FTI, should be protected with a discrete profile. STATISTICS processing is used to determine how that resource is being accessed and how many times it is being accessed. | If access to resource profiles are not audited, unauthorized access to the system and FTI could occur without detection. | The agency should enable the SETROPTS STATISTICS parameter for all active RACF resource classes (ACTIVE CLASSES) defined for FTI resources. |
  | The ATTRIBUTES setting needs improvement | Analysis of the SETROPTS global settings found that OPERAUDIT and INITSTATS are not defined to the ATTRIBUTES operand. The system activities of personnel assigned system-level authorities must be audited at all times by activating INITSTATS, SAUDIT, OPERAUDIT, and CMDVIOL. INITSTATS records statistics on all user profiles in the system. | If the ATTRIBUTES operand does not contain INITSTATS, SAUDIT, OPERAUDIT, and CMDVIOL then RACF will not log all the activities of personnel assigned system-level authorities. Consequently, unauthorized access to the system and FTI could occur without detection. | Enable the SETROPTS ATTRIBUTES operand to include INITSTATS, SAUDIT, OPERAUDIT, and CMDVIOL. |
  | Access controls to SMF audit logs need improvement | Analysis of the access control list associated with SYS1.MAN* (denoted by SYS1.* high-level qualifier) identified the following control deficiencies requiring management attention and prompt corrective action: 1. User Group TSXXXXX has ALTER authority to the SMF audit logs. 2. User Group DPXXX has ALTER authority to the SMF audit logs. 3. User ID TSXXXX has UPDATE authority to the SMF audit logs. | Users with the ALTER access authority can create, modify, or delete the SMS audit logs thereby compromising the integrity of the audit trail. Consequently, unauthorized access to the system and FTI could occur without detection. Users with the UPDATE or READ access authority can access the SMF audit logs and potentially copy these files to their own libraries. Consequently, unauthorized access to the system and FTI could occur without detection. | Remove users and user groups identified with ALTER access authority to the SMF audit logs and develop, approve, and implement written procedures for granting, restricting, and terminating emergency access to SMF audit files to resolve technical contingencies as needed. |

- **Windows**
  - Auditing with Windows Server 2003 and XP is configured in several different ways
  - Auditing is generally turned on through a security policy, which is another part of Group Policy
  - These security policies are generally accessed through Administrative Tools
  - Most common issue: agency does not enable auditing for both “success” and “failure” on the following types:
  
  | Audit type | Description |
  |---|---|
  | Audit Account Logon Events | Tracks user logon and logoff events |
  | Audit Account Management | Reports changes to user accounts |
  | Audit Directory Service Access | Reports access and changes to the directory service. If the system is a member server or XP system, directory service is NTLM-based, and consists of user accounts and group policies |
  | Audit Logon Events | Reports success/failure of any local or remote access-based logon |
  | Audit Object Access | Reports file and folder access. Must be implemented here, and then the individual file/folder must be configured for auditing within its properties in order to fully enable this feature |
  | Audit Policy Change | Reports changes to group policies |
  | Audit Privilege Use | Related to Audit Object Access: reports when permissions are utilized such as read, or full control |
  | Audit System Events | Reports standard system events. Not security related |

  - Second most common issue: agency does not allocate enough storage capacity for these events
  
  | Log size field | Minimum |
  |---|---|
  | Maximum application log size | 16384 kilobytes |
  | Maximum security log size | 81920 kilobytes |
  | Maximum system log size | 16384 kilobytes |

  - Third most common issue: Event Viewer logs are not set to “Do Not Overwrite Events (clear log manually).”
  - This prevents logs from being overwritten and reduces possibility of deletion prior to system admin review or archiving
  - In cases where FTI is stored on a Windows device, it becomes necessary to audit the file or folder access where the FTI resides
  - This is a two part process where the audit policy must be changed, and then the file or folder must be flagged for auditing
  - From that point, items will appear in the Security log of the Event Viewer

  - **Auditing User Access of Files, Folders, and Printers**
    1. Click Start, click Control Panel, click Performance and Maintenance, and then click Administrative Tools.
    2. Double-click Local Security Policy.
    3. In the left pane, double-click Local Policies to expand it.
    4. In the left pane, click Audit Policy to display the individual policy settings in the right pane.
    5. Double-click Audit object access.
    6. To audit successful access of specified files, folders and printers, select the Success check box.
    7. To audit unsuccessful access to these objects, select the Failure check box.
    8. To enable auditing of both, select both check boxes.
    9. Click OK.

  - **Specifying Files, Folders, and Printers to Audit**
    1. In Windows Explorer, locate the file or folder you want to audit. To audit a printer, locate it by clicking Start, and then clicking Printers and Faxes.
    2. Right-click the file, folder, or printer that you want to audit, and then click Properties.
    3. Click the Security tab, and then click Advanced.
    4. Click the Auditing tab, and then click Add.
    5. In the Enter the object name to select box, type the name of the user or group whose access you want to audit. You can browse the computer for names by clicking Advanced, and then clicking Find Now in the Select User or Group dialog box.
    6. Click OK. Select the Successful or Failed check boxes for the actions you want to audit, and then click OK.
    7. Click OK, and then click OK.

- **Cisco routers**
  
  | Finding | Discussion | Risk | Recommendation |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Sequence numbers are not used for syslog messages | Each system status message logged in the system logging process has a sequence reference number applied. The service sequence-numbers command makes that number visible by displaying it with the message. The sequence number is displayed as the first part of the system status message. | Sequence numbering on syslog messages enables an auditing control to indicate if any messages are missing. Without visible sequence numbers some syslog messages may be lost during transmission and would not be accounted for, thus weakening the effectiveness of the system logging. This is turn weakens the integrity of FTI system’s audit trails. | Implement sequence numbering for syslog messages. Recommended commands: `Router#config terminal`; `Router(config)#service sequence-numbers` |
  | NTP authentication is not used | Time synchronization can be authenticated to ensure that the local router obtains its time services only from known sources. By default, network time synchronization is unauthenticated. Uses pre-placed keys to establish a trusted community of NTP servers and peers. Cisco routers support only MD5 authentication for NTP. | With a sophisticated attack, an attacker could use NTP informational queries to discover the timeservers to which a router is synchronized, and then through an attack such as DNS cache poisoning, redirect a router to a system under their control. Manipulating the time on a router this way could make it difficult to identify when incidents truly happened and could also be used to confuse any time-based security measures you have in place. This weakens the integrity of FTI system’s audit trails. | Use NTP authentication between clients, servers, and peers to ensure that time is synchronized to approved servers only. Enable NTP authentication with the `ntp authenticate` command. Define an NTP authentication key with the `ntp authentication-key` command. A unique number identifies each NTP key. This number is the first argument to the `ntp authentication-key` command. Use the `ntp trusted-key` command to tell the router which keys are valid for authentication. The `ntp trusted-key` command's only argument is the number of the key defined in the previous step. To enable authentication on the router and define key number 10: `Router#config terminal`; `Router(config)#ntp authenticate`; `Router(config)#ntp authentication-key 10 md5`; `Router(config)#ntp trusted-key 10`. If external NTP servers require authentication, configure a router to use authentication when contacting those servers by using the `ntp server` command with the key argument. To authenticate NTP peers, configure the same key on both systems and use the `ntp peer` command with the key argument to configure authentication. |
  | Dedicated log servers are not used | Currently a dedicated log server is not used. A host should be configured for the sole purpose of storing logs from the routers. Log servers should be included as a part of network engineering to house and protect the router log files. Log servers should be sized with respect to the amount of traffic produced by the routers on the network, therefore correlating to the amount of log entries routers would produce. | Without a dedicated, protected log server to house the router’s logs, there is risk of logs being deleted or overwritten from the router’s buffered memory before they are able to be analyzed. Security events indicating possible network attacks would go unnoticed allowing the network to be compromised without any advanced warning. | Assign a host as the dedicated log server. The log server should be connected to a trusted or protected network, or an isolated and dedicated router interface. Harden the log host by removing all unnecessary services and accounts. |

title: [PDF] Internal Inspections Report - IRS
content:
- **Document title:** Internal Inspections Report - IRS
- **Template name:** Internal Inspection Template
- **Required location fields**
  - Type of Office:
  - Physical Address:
  - Prepared by:
  - Date:

- **Required signature/acknowledgment fields**
  - Official Conducting Internal Inspection
  - Date
  - Head of Location Being Reviewed
  - Date
  - Agency Reviewer
  - Date

- **Purpose / overall objective**
  - “To measure the level of compliance with Federal disclosure regulations as defined in Pub 1075 and as documented in agency policies and procedures.”

- **Instructions / recurring compliance task execution**
  - Agencies are required to conduct internal inspections as part of their compliance with Publication 1075.
  - The questions serve as an agency internal inspection checklist to identify security procedures and federal security implementation for protecting Federal Tax Information.
  - Document provides:
    - High level questions related directly to Pub 1075 requirements
    - Pub 1075 references
    - Pass/Fail/NA: To notate agency compliance
    - Notes: Location for additional comments specific to the question
  - The agency should complete the contact information below for all parties involved in supplying information for this Internal Inspection.
    - Name
    - Title
    - E-mail
  - Below, please supply the requested information for the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) created as a result of the findings from this Internal Inspection.
    - Date (POA&M) created:
    - Date all Findings from POA&M Remediated:

- **RACI / role responsibilities**
  - Official Conducting Internal Inspection
    - submits Internal Inspection Report to the headquarters function of this agency as part of the IRS Safeguards Internal Inspections requirement
  - Head of Location Being Reviewed
    - acknowledges review of the Internal Inspection Report
    - initiates appropriate corrective actions for any deficiencies identified
  - Agency Reviewer
    - acknowledges review of the Internal Inspection Report

- **Phases / sections / objectives**
  - I. Preliminary
    - Objective: To obtain a general understanding of safeguarding of Federal Taxpayer Information (FTI) in areas being reviewed.
  - II. Record Keeping Requirements (Publication 1075 section 2.A) IRC Section 6103 p 4 A
    - Objective: To ascertain that adequate policies, procedures, and systems are in place to identify, store, protect, and track FTI from receipt to destruction.
  - III. Secure Storage (Publication 1075 section 2.B) IRC Section 6103 p 4 B
    - Objective: To ascertain adequate security of the building or section of building where the FTI is located.
  - IV. Restricting Access (Publication 1075 section 2.C) IRC Section 6103(p)(4)(C)
    - Objective: To determine whether access to FTI is adequately controlled and restricted.
  - V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information Publication 1075 section 2.F IRC Section 6103 p 4 F
    - Objective: To determine if FTI is disposed of properly.
  - VI. Cybersecurity Requirements
    - Objective: To determine if information technology security and privacy requirements are met to adequately protect FTI.
  - VI. Conclusion
    - A. The agency must implement a process for ensuring that a POA&M is developed and monitored in accordance with Pub 1075.
    - B. Complete Internal Inspection Report
    - C. Retain Internal Inspection Report for 5 years

- **Checklist / operational questions and fields captured**

| Section | Item | Required information / question |
|---|---|---|
| I. Preliminary | A | Complete the Internal Inspection Document |
| I. Preliminary | B | Obtain and review a copy of last internal inspection report. Follow up on open items from the previous inspection. |
| I. Preliminary | C | Obtain a list of all FTI (paper/electronic) housed at this location |
| I. Preliminary | C | Paper FTI received/created |
| I. Preliminary | C | Electronic FTI received/created |
| I. Preliminary | D | Obtain and review a list of all employees/contractors with authorized access to FTI. The list must contain: |
| I. Preliminary | D | FTI access by individual name |
| I. Preliminary | D | Use of access by individual name |
| I. Preliminary | E | Obtain and review the policies and procedures for safeguarding FTI. |
| II. Record Keeping Requirements | A | Is the paper FTI recorded/tracked in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| II. Record Keeping Requirements | B | Is the electronic FTI recorded/tracked in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| II. Record Keeping Requirements | C | Does the agency disclose to state auditors? If the agency discloses to state auditors, do the agency log in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| II. Record Keeping Requirements | D | Does the agency retain the FTI logs in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | A | Does the physical security provide two barriers to prevent unauthorized access to FTI? (in accordance with Pub 1075 requirements for Minimum Protection Standards-MPS) |
| III. Secure Storage | B | Does the agency follow the requirements for visitor access logs in accordance with Pub 1075 for areas containing FTI? Are visitor logs closed and reviewed at least monthly in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | C | Does the agency use an authorized access list (AAL) for access to FTI? Is the AAL maintained in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | D | Are non-AAL visitors escorted in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | E | Review physical security and key/combination/electronic controls and verify they are in accordance with Pub 1075. |
| III. Secure Storage | F | Are records on key/combination/electronic access cards maintained in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | G | Are authorized personnel required to wear an identification badge when serving as a secondary barrier for FTI in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | H | Is FTI safeguarded in accordance with Pub 1075 when in transit (offsite storage, other offices, etc.)? |
| III. Secure Storage | I | Is the FTI, sent to an offsite storage facility, protected from access by unauthorized individuals at all times? (If the answer is no, offsite storage facility must be reviewed.) |
| III. Secure Storage | J | Are employees allowed to work at an alternate work site? Is the FTI, at the alternate work site, safeguarded in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| III. Secure Storage | K | Does the agency retain ownership and control of all hardware, software and end-point equipment receiving, storing, processing or transmitting FTI? If the answer is no, is the agency using Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI)? |
| IV. Restricting Access | A | Is access to FTI restricted to only authorized personnel who have a need to know? |
| IV. Restricting Access | B | Is all FTI clearly labeled “Federal Tax Information” in accordance with Pub 1075 (paper and electronic)? |
| IV. Restricting Access | C | Has the agency initiated background investigations for all employees and contractors with access to FTI in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| IV. Restricting Access | D | Is FTI commingled with other information? Can FTI within agency records be located and separated easily? |
| IV. Restricting Access | E | Is FTI disclosed to personnel outside of the agency (contractors, other agencies, etc.)? Are the disclosures tracked in accordance with Pub 1075? List personnel/offices (which FTI is disclosed). |
| IV. Restricting Access | F | Are personnel following the agency policy for transmitting FTI via email? (policy in preliminary section) |
| IV. Restricting Access | G | Are personnel following the agency policy for transmitting FTI via fax? (policy in preliminary section) |
| V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information | A | Does the agency return FTI to the IRS when no longer needed? |
| V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information | B | Does the agency destroy paper FTI in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information | C | Does the agency destroy electronic FTI in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information | D | Does the agency sanitize physical media containing FTI before it leaves the physical or systemic control of the agency? |
| V. Disposing Federal Taxpayer Information | E | Does the agency ensure FTI is not disclosed during disposal processes? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | A | Does the agency perform vulnerability assessments in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | B | Does the agency require multi-factor authentication for remote access in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | C | Does the agency encrypt FTI in the LAN in accordance with Pub 1075? Provide a description of how the FTI is encrypted. |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | D | Does the agency follow the process for changes to information systems in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | E | Does the agency manage their information accounts in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | F | Does the agency implement auditing procedures on information systems in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | G | Does the agency manage information system authenticators in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | H | Does the agency have standard baseline configurations for information systems processing FTI in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | I | Does the agency maintain active vendor support for all devices on its network? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | J | Does the agency have a current inventory of all information system components in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | K | Does the agency maintain a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) in accordance with Pub 1075? |
| VI. Cybersecurity Requirements | L | Does the agency assess the security controls in the information system and its environment in accordance with Pub 1075? |

title: Safeguards technical assistance memorandum STAX audit ...
content:
## Operational runbook / SOP structure
- **Source reference**
  - IRS Publication 1075
  - Section **5.6.2**
  - **Exhibit 9**

## Recurring security/compliance task execution
- **Audit logs**
  - Audit logs should be archived and stored on a central log server where access can be restricted through system permissions.
  - If logs are configured to automatically archive and transmit to a central server for storage, the risk of exceeding audit log storage capacity and overwriting logs on the STAX system is mitigated.
- **Audit information retention**
  - IRS Publication 1075 requires all agencies ensure that audit information is archived for **six years** to enable the recreation of computer-related accesses to both the operating system and to the application wherever FTI is stored.
- **Storage guidance**
  - There is no specific Publication 1075 requirement that logs must be stored in paper and CD format.
  - It is recommended that audit logs **not** be stored in paper format to minimize the potential for the audit data being compromised.
  - CD is an acceptable storage format for audit logs.
  - It is recommended that **write-once media** be used to ensure that log files are not inadvertently erased and integrity of the files is maintained.
- **Physical security if CDs are used**
  - CDs used for storage of audit logs are subject to Publication 1075 Minimum Protection Standards for physical security of **two barrier rule** for access to FTI under normal security:
    - Secured perimeter/locked container
    - Locked perimeter/secured interior
    - Locked perimeter/security container

## Audit evidence / artifacts
- **Audit logs**
  - Records of system and network security
  - May contain sensitive information regarding transactions with FTI
- **Archived audit information**
  - Must be archived for **six years**
  - Enables recreation of computer-related accesses to:
    - Operating system
    - Application wherever FTI is stored

## POA&M / remediation records
- **Not stated in page**

## RACI / role responsibilities
- **Management of audit logs**
  - Should be handled by individuals that are **not users/administrators** of the systems for which the logs are kept.
  - Ideally, an **agency security office** would perform the audit log activities to provide an “independence” or “separation of duties”.
  - If an agency’s Disclosure and Security Offices have consolidated and an agency security office is not possible, the agency should designate **someone in the newly consolidated office** with responsibility for managing the system audit logs.
  - The newly assigned individual/s **must not have administrator rights** on the system/s being audited.

## Task / ticket / playbook templates
- **Not stated in page**

## Escalation / exception handling
- If the agency’s Disclosure and Security Offices have consolidated, the ideal separation of duties arrangement may not be possible.
- In that case, the agency should designate someone in the newly consolidated office with responsibility for managing the system audit logs.
- The designated individual/s must not have administrator rights on the system/s being audited.

## Cadence / frequency
- **Audit information archived for six years**
- No other recurring cadence or schedule stated.

## Fields captured
- **Not stated in page**

## Named standards / references
- IRS Publication 1075
- NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management
- NIST SP 800-53, Recommended Security Controls for Federal Information Systems

## Specific requirements and storage/security details
| Item | Explicit details |
|---|---|
| Paper copy requirement for STAX log | No specific Publication 1075 requirement states the logs must be stored in paper and CD format |
| Paper storage recommendation | Audit logs are recommended not to be stored in paper format |
| CD storage acceptability | CD is an acceptable storage format for audit logs |
| Media recommendation | Write-once media is recommended for CDs |
| Physical security for CDs | Subject to Publication 1075 Minimum Protection Standards for physical security of two barrier rule for access to FTI under normal security |
| Two barrier rule options | Secured perimeter/locked container; Locked perimeter/secured interior; Locked perimeter/security container |
| Locked definition | An area or container that has a lock and the keys or combinations are controlled |
| Security container definition | A lockable metal container with a resistance to forced penetration, with a security lock and keys or combinations are controlled |
| Central log server | Ideally logs would be archived and stored on a central log server |
| Benefit of auto-archive/transmit | Mitigates the risk of exceeding audit log storage capacity and overwriting logs on the STAX system |
